entry.title: Umbrellas in a cage
entry.content:
A molecule of ammonia, started in one shape, tunnels inside out and back about twenty-four billion times a second, through an energy barrier it does not have enough energy to climb. This post is about two of its cousins, and about what happens to that flip when you lock the molecule inside a cage of sixty carbon atoms.

The paper this post is about asks a narrow question: if you take a small, pyramid-shaped molecule that likes to flip inside out, and shut it inside a C₆₀ fullerene, does the flip get easier or harder, and why? We looked at two molecules, the hydronium ion (OH₃⁺, the thing that makes acids acidic) and phosphine (PH₃), and the answer turned out to be different for each . The work was done at Krea University with Dr Brijesh Kumar Mishra and Dr Sivakumar Srinivasan, together with Shreya Chidambaram and Netra Krishna.

I came to this project without having done any quantum chemistry. I had to teach myself how to use ORCA, what a basis set was, why there were dozens of “functionals” with names like B3LYP and M06-2X, and how to keep a cluster busy without breaking it. So this post is written for someone in roughly the position I was in: you have done some physics and chemistry, you have heard the words “quantum tunnelling” and “DFT”, and you would like to know what they actually mean. The first third builds up the idea of inversion and tunnelling, the middle third is a tour of how molecules are calculated, and the last third puts the two together to read the paper’s results. The practical side, how I learned ORCA and ran these jobs on a cluster, will get a post of its own.

An umbrella in the wind

Ammonia, NH₃, is shaped like a short, squat pyramid: a nitrogen atom on top, three hydrogens forming the base. The nitrogen also carries a pair of electrons that are not shared with anything, a “lone pair”, which sits on the side away from the hydrogens and pushes them down, a bit like the canopy of an umbrella with the handle being the lone pair.

Now imagine the umbrella in a strong wind. The canopy goes flat, and then pops through to the other side. A pyramidal molecule can do the same thing: the central atom passes through the plane of the three hydrogens and comes out on the other side, and you end up with the same pyramid, pointing the other way. This is called umbrella inversion, and the halfway point, where the molecule is completely flat, is the hardest part of the journey.

The two molecules in the paper make a useful pair. Hydronium is a water molecule that has picked up an extra proton. It is positively charged, it is flatter than ammonia (the H–O–H angle is about 112°, against about 107° in ammonia), and it flips easily. Phosphine is ammonia with the nitrogen swapped for phosphorus, the next element down the same column of the periodic table. Its bonds are longer, and its H–P–H angle is only about 93°, so it is a tall, narrow pyramid, and it almost never flips. The reason the angles differ so much is a story about how much the phosphorus 3s and 3p orbitals mix, which I will leave aside here; what matters for us is that one of these molecules sits near the easy end of inversion, and the other near the hard end.

Two valleys and a hill

To say anything quantitative, we need to talk about energy. Picture a line along which the molecule flips, from “pyramid pointing up”, through “flat”, to “pyramid pointing down”, and plot the molecule’s energy at each point along it. The two pyramids are equally comfortable, so they sit at the bottoms of two identical valleys. The flat shape is strained, so it sits at the top of a hill between them. Chemists call this a double-well potential, the top of the hill is the transition state, and the height of the hill above the valley floor is the inversion barrier.

The horizontal axis needs a name, and the paper calls it the reaction coordinate. Informally, it measures how far the molecule is from flat, and which way it is pointing. (Formally, it is a “mass-weighted” distance, measured in units of bohr·amu½, which takes into account that it is mostly the light hydrogens that move. You can ignore the units and think of it as “umbrella-ness”.)

A detour on units

Spectroscopists measure energies in wavenumbers, cm⁻¹, which looks strange for an energy. The idea is that light of a given energy has a given wavelength, and the wavenumber is just how many of those wavelengths fit into a centimetre, so higher wavenumber means higher energy. Some conversions to hold on to: 1 kcal/mol is about 350 cm⁻¹, and the typical thermal energy available to a molecule at room temperature, kBT, is about 208 cm⁻¹.

On that scale, the hydronium barrier of about 700 cm⁻¹ is only about three and a half times the thermal energy, and the phosphine barrier of about 11,600 cm⁻¹ is more than fifty times it.

If molecules behaved like balls rolling on a landscape, the story would end here. A ball with less energy than the hill would roll back and forth inside one valley forever. A ball with more would roll over the top. The barrier would be a wall, and only molecules that were hot enough would ever flip.

Going through the hill

Molecules are not balls, though, and at this scale the rules are quantum mechanical. Two things change.

The first is that a molecule cannot have any energy it likes. Confined to a valley, it can only have certain energies, the energy levels, and it can never sit perfectly still at the bottom: even the lowest level sits some way above the valley floor (this leftover energy is called the zero-point energy). Each level comes with a wavefunction, ψ, whose square tells you how likely you are to find the molecule at each point along the reaction coordinate.

The second change is the one that matters for inversion. A wavefunction does not stop dead at the edge of a valley. It leaks into the hill, fading away exponentially, and if the hill is thin enough and low enough, a little of it reaches the other side. So the molecule does not have to climb over the barrier to get to the other valley; there is a probability that it is simply found on the other side. This is quantum tunnelling.

One consequence is beautiful and is what you can actually measure. Because the two valleys are identical, the wavefunctions have to be either symmetric (the same on both sides, labelled +) or antisymmetric (equal and opposite, labelled −). Without tunnelling, those two would have exactly the same energy. With tunnelling, they are split apart by a small amount, the tunnelling splitting, ΔE, and each level becomes a closely spaced pair, a doublet. Friedrich Hund worked out this picture in 1927 , and it was soon used to explain a doubling of lines in ammonia’s spectrum . Ammonia’s ground-state splitting is about 0.79 cm⁻¹, which corresponds to a microwave frequency of about 23.8 GHz, and that is where the opening line of this post comes from. One of ammonia’s inversion lines near that frequency is also what the first maser, built in 1954, ran on .

The splitting is extraordinarily sensitive to the shape of the barrier. Make the hill a little higher or a little wider, and the splitting does not shrink a little; it shrinks exponentially. That sensitivity is why inversion is a good probe of the environment a molecule is in, and it is the thing to play with below.

There is another way to see what a splitting means. If you could prepare the molecule so that it is definitely in the left valley, that state is not one of the energy levels but a mixture of the + and − states of a pair. Left alone, the mixture does not stay put: it sloshes into the right valley and back again, and the time it takes to go there and back is set by the splitting, T = h/ΔE. A large splitting means fast sloshing, and a tiny splitting means the molecule stays where it is for a very long time.

For hydronium the back-and-forth takes well under a picosecond. For phosphine, which has a much higher and wider barrier, the calculated splitting is so small (well below 10⁻¹¹ cm⁻¹, with estimates that span several orders of magnitude depending on how you compute it) that the round trip would take anywhere from seconds to about a day, which on a molecular timescale is close to forever. No inversion splitting has ever been seen in phosphine’s spectrum, although full-dimensional calculations suggest it might show up in highly excited bending states . One of our molecules is a fast tunneller, and the other is, for practical purposes, stuck.

A cage made of carbon

C₆₀ is a hollow ball of sixty carbon atoms, arranged in twelve pentagons and twenty hexagons exactly like the panels of a football. It was discovered in 1985 , and its carbon atoms sit on a sphere about 7 Å across. Once you allow for the size of the carbon atoms’ own electron clouds, that leaves an empty space in the middle only about 3.7 Å across, and chemists have found ways to put things in it. Molecules inside fullerenes are called endohedral, and they are written with an @ sign, so a water molecule inside C₆₀ is H₂O@C₆₀.

This is not only a thought experiment. Using a sequence of reactions sometimes called “molecular surgery”, chemists open a hole in the cage, slip a molecule in, and stitch the hole closed again. Hydrogen was put inside C₆₀ in 2005 , and water in 2011 , and once inside, these molecules keep rotating and vibrating while held away from everything else. They have become a kind of laboratory for studying a single molecule in a very clean, very small box.

That raises a question. If tunnelling is so sensitive to the shape of the barrier, what does the box do to it? Physicists have known since the 1940s that squeezing a quantum oscillator into a box pushes its energy levels up , but a flip is a more delicate thing than a single vibration. Does squeezing a molecule make it harder to flip, because there is less room, or easier, because of how the cage pulls on it? Is the answer the same for a charged molecule and a neutral one? Our group had already looked at ammonia inside C₆₀ , and this paper asks the same questions for hydronium and phosphine.

To answer the question, though, we have to be able to calculate the double well for a molecule that is surrounded by sixty carbon atoms. That needs a detour into how molecules are calculated at all.

How do you calculate a molecule?

Everything about a molecule, its shape, its energy, how it vibrates, follows in principle from one equation, the Schrödinger equation. The trouble is in the words “in principle”.

The first simplification is the Born–Oppenheimer approximation. Nuclei are thousands of times heavier than electrons, so the electrons rearrange themselves almost instantly whenever the nuclei move. That means you can freeze the nuclei in place, solve for the electrons, and get an energy for that one arrangement of nuclei. Do that for many arrangements and you get a potential energy surface, and the double well from the last section is a slice through exactly such a surface.

So the real problem is the electrons. The difficulty is that the electrons all repel each other, so the position of every electron depends on where all the others are, and the wavefunction that describes them is a function of all their coordinates at once: three coordinates per electron. Hydronium has 10 electrons, so its wavefunction is a function of 30 variables. C₆₀ has 360 electrons, so its wavefunction lives in 1,080 dimensions. You cannot store such a thing, let alone solve for it directly.

Every practical method in quantum chemistry is a way of approximating this problem, and they trade accuracy for cost in different ways. Two families matter for this paper.

Hartree–Fock, and what it leaves out

The oldest approach is the Hartree–Fock method. Instead of letting every electron respond to every other electron individually, it lets each electron move in the average field of all the others. Each electron then gets its own wavefunction, an orbital, and these are the orbitals you meet in chemistry classes. The catch is that the average field depends on the orbitals, and the orbitals depend on the field, so the method goes round in a loop: guess the orbitals, build the field, solve for new orbitals, rebuild the field, and repeat until nothing changes. This loop is called the self-consistent field (SCF), and DFT uses the same idea.

What Hartree–Fock leaves out is that real electrons dodge each other on the fly, rather than just feeling an average. The energy that comes from this dodging is called the correlation energy. It is a small fraction of the total, but chemistry happens in small differences, so it matters a great deal. One part of it matters for this paper in particular: dispersion, the weak, attractive “London” force that arises when the electrons of two neighbouring molecules fluctuate in step with each other. It is why noble gases liquefy at all, and Hartree–Fock does not capture it.

Methods that add correlation back on top of Hartree–Fock are called post-Hartree–Fock, or wavefunction methods. MP2 adds it as a correction using perturbation theory. Coupled cluster goes much further, and the version known as CCSD(T), which treats single and double excitations of electrons in full and adds triple excitations approximately , is often called the “gold standard” of quantum chemistry, because for well-behaved molecules, with a large enough basis set, it gets energies right to within about a kilocalorie per mole. It is also very expensive. Its cost grows roughly as the seventh power of the size of the system, so doubling the size of a molecule makes the calculation about a hundred and twenty-eight times slower.

Density functional theory

Density functional theory (DFT) comes at the problem from the other end. In 1964, Hohenberg and Kohn proved something surprising: the ground-state energy of a system of electrons is completely determined by its electron density, the three-dimensional function from the figure above . You do not need the 3N-dimensional wavefunction to get the energy, in principle; the density, which is a function of only three coordinates, contains all the information.

The catch is that the proof says such a mapping from density to energy, a functional, exists, but not what it is. A year later, Kohn and Sham found a practical route . They imagined a fictitious system of electrons that do not interact with each other but have exactly the same density as the real ones. For non-interacting electrons, almost everything can be calculated exactly, and all the difficult many-body physics gets pushed into one leftover term, the exchange–correlation functional. If we knew that term exactly, DFT would be exact. We do not, and the hundreds of “functionals” in use today, with names like B3LYP, PBE0, M06-2X and B97-D, are different approximations to it. John Perdew described them as rungs on a “Jacob’s ladder”, climbing from simple approximations towards the exact answer, with each rung costing more .

In practice, DFT costs roughly as much as Hartree–Fock but includes a good part of the correlation energy, which is why it is the workhorse of computational chemistry. Its weaknesses are that there is no systematic way to improve a given functional, so you have to check how a functional does on problems similar to yours, and that most functionals miss dispersion too. They include correlation, but they work out the energy by looking at the density at and near each point, while dispersion is a correlation between electrons that are far apart. Stefan Grimme’s fix was pragmatic: add a simple, empirically fitted attraction between every pair of atoms that falls off as 1/r⁶, the way dispersion does. The functional we ended up using, B97-D, is one he built with that correction included from the start . For a molecule sitting inside a cage of sixty carbon atoms, dispersion is not a detail.

Basis sets

There is one more ingredient, and it is the part of a method’s name after the slash. Orbitals are smooth functions in three-dimensional space, and computers work with finite lists of numbers, so every calculation builds its orbitals out of a fixed set of simpler functions, a basis set, and only solves for how much of each to mix in.

The natural building blocks would be functions shaped like the orbitals of the hydrogen atom, which fall off as e−r. But the integrals that a calculation needs are much faster to compute with Gaussian functions, e−αr², so almost all of quantum chemistry builds its orbitals out of sums of Gaussians. A single Gaussian is the wrong shape: it is too flat at the nucleus, where the true orbital has a sharp point, and it dies away too quickly far from it. Add a few with different widths, and the sum gets close.

The basis sets in this paper have names like aug-cc-pVTZ, which unpacks as follows. cc-p means “correlation-consistent polarised”, a family designed by Thom Dunning so that results improve systematically as the sets get bigger . VTZ means valence triple-zeta: each valence orbital gets three functions of different sizes, so it can stretch or contract as the bonding demands. Polarised means there are also functions of higher angular momentum (d and f functions on a carbon atom, say) so that orbitals can bend and distort. And aug means augmented with very spread-out “diffuse” functions , which matter for ions, for weak interactions, and for the outer, loosely held parts of a molecule’s electron cloud. QZ, quadruple-zeta, is the next size up, and the larger the basis, the closer you get to the answer the method would give with a perfect basis, and the more it costs.

Why the cage needed DFT

Now the practical problem is clear. A free hydronium ion in the aug-cc-pVTZ basis is a small calculation. Put it inside C₆₀ and you add sixty carbon atoms, each of which brings its own set of basis functions, and the calculation is more than twenty times bigger. For a method whose cost grows as the seventh power of size, that is not a factor of twenty; it is a factor of billions.

So the paper splits the work. For the free molecules, which are small, we computed CCSD(T) energies with the large aug-cc-pVQZ basis along the path, to get the most reliable double wells we could, and compared them against experiment where experiment exists. For the caged molecules, the full double well had to come from DFT. And to check the strength of the binding between the guest and the cage, which needs high accuracy at only a few geometries, we used DLPNO-CCSD(T), a local approximation to coupled cluster developed in Frank Neese’s group, the group behind ORCA , which makes coupled-cluster-quality energies possible for systems the size of a fullerene.

Choosing a functional

Which DFT functional, then? This is where one has to be careful. In our earlier work on ammonia inside C₆₀, the M06-2X functional had reproduced the experimental inversion barrier well , so the obvious move would have been to use it again. Before trusting any functional, though, we tested several of them against CCSD(T)/aug-cc-pVQZ on the free molecules, where both could be computed.

For phosphine, almost everything gets the barrier right to within about 7%. For hydronium, the methods are all over the place, and M06-2X, which had done so well for ammonia, gives a barrier a third to a half too low, depending on the basis set. B97-D with the aug-cc-pVTZ basis was the only functional that did well on both molecules, so that is what we used for the caged systems. It is still about 13% low for hydronium (612 against 706 cm⁻¹), which is worth remembering when we get to the results.

I find this one of the more useful lessons of the project, and it is the one I would pass on to anyone starting out the way I did. There is no “best functional”. There is the functional that has been shown to work for your kind of problem, and the only way to know is to check.

Tracing the path

With the method chosen, the calculation of a double well goes through a few steps, each of which is a standard job type in a program like ORCA or Gaussian.

First, geometry optimisation: start from a rough guess of the pyramid and let the program move the atoms downhill until the forces on them vanish. That gives the bottom of a valley. Second, find the transition state, the flat geometry at the top of the hill. A transition state is a saddle point: it is a maximum along the reaction coordinate and a minimum in every other direction. A frequency calculation confirms which is which, because a true minimum has only real vibrational frequencies, while a transition state has exactly one imaginary frequency, whose motion is the flip itself. The barrier height is then just the difference in energy between the two.

Third, the path between them. An intrinsic reaction coordinate (IRC) calculation starts at the transition state and follows the steepest way down, in mass-weighted coordinates, until it reaches the valley . That gives one half of the double well, from the top of the hill to the bottom of the valley. But the wavefunctions also spread up the far wall of each valley, the side where the pyramid is squashed taller than its equilibrium shape, so we ran a second set of IRC calculations starting from compressed pyramids and following them back down. Joining the two pieces, and using the fact that the two valleys are mirror images, gives the whole double well.

Fourth, a smooth curve through the points. The paper fits each double well to the form

$$V(x) = A x^4 + B\, e^{-C x^2} - D x^2,$$

a quartic wall that keeps the molecule from flying apart, a Gaussian bump for the barrier in the middle, and an inverted parabola that deepens the two valleys. (The paper writes the last term as +Dx² with a negative D; I have written the minus sign explicitly.) The constant B is the energy of the flat geometry, x = 0, and it equals the barrier height when the valley floors sit at zero.

Finally, the quantum part. With V(x) in hand, the one-dimensional Schrödinger equation for motion along x can be solved numerically for the energy levels and wavefunctions, which the paper does with the shooting method. This is exactly the calculation the playground earlier in this post is running in your browser, and solving it with the fitted parameters from the paper reproduces the paper’s lowest energy levels to within a few cm⁻¹, and the higher ones to within about half a per cent.

What the cage does

Here is the main result, with the double wells for both molecules, free and caged.

Hydronium gets stuck. Inside C₆₀, the B97-D barrier for hydronium rises from 612 to about 870 cm⁻¹, and the two valleys move further apart (the pyramid gets about 25% taller). Both changes make tunnelling harder, and the ground-state splitting falls from 104 to 38 cm⁻¹, a drop by almost two-thirds. For the free molecule, B97-D overestimates the splitting compared with experiment (104 against 55 cm⁻¹), while CCSD(T) gets much closer (49 to 65 cm⁻¹ depending on the basis set), so the absolute numbers for the caged molecule should not be taken too literally. The direction and the rough size of the effect, though, are what DFT should get right, since the same method is being compared with itself.

Why would the valleys move apart? Our interpretation in the paper is that it comes from the charge. Hydronium is a cation, and its positive charge pulls the electron cloud of the cage towards it, inducing a negative charge on the inner surface of the C₆₀. The ion is then attracted to that induced charge, and the attraction favours the pyramidal shapes over the flat one. That is an interpretation, and the paper does not test it separately.

Phosphine barely notices. Phosphine’s barrier was already enormous, and confinement lowers it only slightly, from about 11,600 to 11,000 cm⁻¹. It is still more than fifty times room-temperature thermal energy, and tunnelling stays negligible inside the cage as well as outside it. What changes is mostly the shape of the well: phosphine’s umbrella vibration shifts up a little (1027 to 1056 cm⁻¹), and the spacing between its energy levels grows slightly, which is what you would expect if the walls of the well get a little steeper.

So the same cage does opposite things to the two molecules. For the charged, floppy hydronium, it raises the barrier and suppresses tunnelling. For the neutral, rigid phosphine, it lowers the barrier slightly and otherwise changes very little.

The geometries and vibrations tell the same story. In the cage, hydronium’s O–H bonds stretch slightly (0.982 to 0.995 Å) and their stretching vibrations shift to lower frequencies, while the bending motion that drives the flip stiffens (842 to 1037 cm⁻¹). Phosphine’s P–H bonds shorten (1.428 to 1.396 Å) and all of its vibrations shift to higher frequencies, which is what you would expect of a molecule that is being pressed on from all sides. The cage itself barely moves: the carbon atoms shift by only about 0.07 Å (root-mean-square) when a guest is inside.

What holds them in

Is the molecule actually stable in there, or would it rather be outside? The interaction energy answers that: the energy of the guest inside the cage, minus the energies of the guest and the empty cage apart. A negative number means the combination is more stable than the two pieces.

With DLPNO-CCSD(T), the interaction energy is −30.8 kcal/mol for hydronium and −13.4 kcal/mol for phosphine . Both are bound, hydronium much more strongly. (B97-D gets hydronium about right, but underestimates phosphine’s binding by nearly a factor of two, which is a useful caution about using one method for everything.)

To see why they are bound, we split the interaction energy into physically meaningful pieces using the local energy decomposition (LED) built into ORCA . It is easiest to read as a budget.

Both molecules have to pay a large up-front cost, the electronic preparation energy, to squeeze their electron clouds into the space and to let the cage’s electrons rearrange around them. That cost is larger for phosphine (174.5 against 117.8 kcal/mol), because phosphine is the bigger molecule. They pay it back in different ways. Hydronium is held mostly by electrostatics, which makes sense for a positive ion surrounded by a polarisable cloud of 360 electrons. Phosphine gets a larger share of its binding from dispersion (38.9 against 18.3 kcal/mol), along with exchange and polarisation, the soft, correlated attraction that Hartree–Fock misses and that Grimme’s correction was designed to add back.

What this does not tell us

It is worth being plain about the limits of all this.

The double wells are one-dimensional. A real molecule has many ways to vibrate, and the umbrella motion is coupled to the others; for free hydronium, full-dimensional calculations have shown that the coupling is strong . Reducing inversion to a single coordinate captures the essentials, but the numbers it gives are those of a model.

The caged results come from DFT, and the free-molecule benchmarks show that B97-D underestimates hydronium’s barrier and overestimates its splitting. The comparison between free and caged is made with the same method on both sides, which is why I trust the direction of the effects more than their exact sizes, but I cannot rule out that the method’s errors behave differently inside the cage.

The phosphine splittings are so small that they sit at the edge of what these calculations can resolve. The paper itself points out that the computed values depend strongly on the method and that tiny numerical noise along the flat part of the potential can be amplified when the curve is interpolated. I would read the phosphine splittings as “negligible, free or caged”, and not put weight on any single number.

And these are calculations on idealised systems. As far as I know, neither OH₃⁺@C₆₀ nor PH₃@C₆₀ has been made in a laboratory (even ammonia inside C₆₀ was still described as a target in 2022), and a real sample of a caged cation would also have a counter-ion somewhere nearby, which our model does not include. So the predictions here are waiting for an experiment, and I would be curious to see whether the suppression of hydronium’s tunnelling shows up in a spectrum.

Coming back to it

What I find satisfying about this problem is how much of physical chemistry it touches with so few atoms. A four-atom molecule and a ball of carbon are enough to bring in potential energy surfaces, tunnelling, the particle in a box, the whole ladder of electronic structure methods, and the question of where binding comes from, and the answers are not the same for two molecules that look almost alike on paper.

It also raises questions I do not know the answers to. If a charged guest polarises the cage and that changes its barrier, could you tune a guest’s tunnelling by changing the cage, say with a larger fullerene, or one with a metal atom or a different charge? Would an external electric field, pushing on the induced charge, do something similar? And how well does the one-dimensional picture hold up once the cage is allowed to vibrate along with the guest?

Behind every number in this post is a lot of practical work that does not appear in the paper: input files, convergence failures, jobs that ran for days on a cluster and then had to be run again. I learned most of that by doing it badly first, and I want to write it up properly, which is what the next post will be about.
entry.summary: Some small molecules turn themselves inside out like an umbrella in the wind, and quantum mechanics lets them do it through a wall of energy they cannot climb. A visual walk through my paper on what happens to that flip when the molecule is shut inside a C₆₀ football, and an introduction to how chemists calculate any of this, density functional theory included.

entry.title: The quiet injury
entry.content:
Somewhere in the world, about once or twice every second, a force from outside the body changes how somebody’s brain works. Most of those people are told the injury is mild, many walk out of the emergency department with a normal scan, and for a good number of them that is not the end of it.
0 people have had a traumatic brain injury since you opened this page, going by the lowest of the global estimates. The highest would make it about two and a half times as many.
Part 1The quiet injury Part 2Thinking in graphs Part 3A map of what comes after

In 2023, for my undergraduate capstone at Krea University, I spent a few months with a database of people who had been through a traumatic brain injury in the United States, trying to work out which other illnesses tended to turn up together in the years afterwards. The project was supervised by Dr Shyam Kumar Sudhakar, and it led to a paper on how common those illnesses were five years after a mild injury , a perspective piece on why graph theory might help , and a paper that built the illnesses into networks . This series is my attempt to explain that work to someone who has never studied medicine, statistics or graph theory, which, at the start of the project, was more or less me.

Before I can get to networks, though, I need you to care about the injury, and in my experience most people do not think about brain injury at all unless it has happened to someone they know. This first part is about the injury itself: how common it is, what physically happens inside a head when it is struck or shaken, why the word “mild” misleads, and why the people who study it have started to describe it as a disease that goes on for years rather than as an event that is over once the bruise fades. Part 2 builds the graph-theory toolkit from scratch, and Part 3 puts the two together.

An ordinary injury

The consensus definition is broad on purpose. A traumatic brain injury (TBI) is “an alteration in brain function, or other evidence of brain pathology, caused by an external force” . The force can be a blow, the head hitting the ground, a sudden stop in a car, a blast, or a penetrating object, and the alteration can be anything from a few minutes of confusion to a coma. My thesis used a textbook wording that I still like because it spells out what can be affected: damage to the brain from an external mechanical force, “resulting in either temporary or permanent impairment of physical, cognitive, and psychosocial functions, as well as alterations or reductions in consciousness” .

How many people does this happen to? The honest answer is that nobody knows to within a factor of two or so. The Global Burden of Disease study estimated 27.08 million new cases in 2016 . The Lancet Neurology Commission on TBI puts it at 50 to 60 million a year, and points out the gap with the GBD figure itself . A third estimate, built from a different set of studies, comes to 69 million . The Commission also says that “of all common neurological disorders, TBI has the highest incidence” .

Much of the spread comes from the fact that most brain injuries are mild, and much mild injury never reaches a hospital, so any estimate built from hospital records misses a large share of it. The WHO’s task force on mild TBI put the hospital-treated rate at about 100 to 300 per 100,000 people a year, and the true population rate at “probably above 600/100,000” . A Canadian study of concussion found 1,153 per 100,000 per year . Between 70 and 90 per cent of treated brain injuries are mild , and the Commission puts it at more than 90 per cent of all cases . So when you read a number for TBI, it is mostly a number for mild TBI, and it is probably an undercount.

The cost is easier to pin down than the count. The Commission puts it at around US$400 billion a year to the global economy, and in Europe alone more than two million people are admitted to hospital with TBI each year and about 82,000 die . In the United States in 2013 there were about 2.8 million TBI-related emergency visits, hospitalisations and deaths . One self-reported estimate quoted in the textbook my thesis leaned on has lifetime prevalence at up to 40% of adults , which I find hard to square with how rarely anyone mentions having had one. I suspect that is because a large part of it is the kind of thing people describe as “I hit my head” and then stop thinking about.

Who, how and where

Who gets hurt, and how, depends a great deal on where they live and how old they are. In high-income countries most TBI comes from falls, “particularly in older people (aged ≥65 years), who often have comorbidities” . In the United States the highest rates of TBI-related emergency visits, hospitalisations and deaths were in people aged 75 and over (2,232.2 per 100,000), followed by the very young (0 to 4) and people aged 15 to 24, and falls in the over-75s drove much of the rise in emergency visits between 2007 and 2013 . In low- and middle-income countries the picture is driven by road traffic, “particularly those involving motorcyclists” . Globally, falls were 52% of causes in 1990 and 54% in 2019 .

India deserves its own paragraph, partly because I live here and partly because the numbers are so thin. The estimate that is still cited most often is from 2002: “nearly 1.5 to 2 million persons are injured” every year, with road traffic the leading cause at about 60%, followed by falls at 20 to 25% and violence at about 10%, and alcohol involved in 15 to 20% of cases . That a twenty-year-old figure is still the reference point is itself a finding. A 2017 systematic review pooled 72 studies of 19,962 patients from 14 states over 27 years and found a mean age of 31.3, a male to female ratio of 3.8 to 1, and a mean in-hospital mortality of 24.6%; it also noted that “over a quarter of the world’s trauma deaths occur in India, with traumatic brain injury (TBI) as the leading cause of death and disability within trauma”, and that the quality of reporting was low . Road traffic accounted for 55.5% of the injuries in that review and falls for 29.2% .

What happens after the injury differs just as much. A comparison in the Commission’s report is the starkest pair of numbers I came across while reading for this series.

Hold on to that second pair. The database my project used is made up entirely of people who were discharged to inpatient rehabilitation in the United States, which, in India, would describe almost nobody.

A soft thing in a hard box

To see why a blow that leaves the skull intact can still hurt the brain, it helps to know what kind of object the brain is, physically. It is very soft. When engineers press on slices of brain to measure how stiff it is, they find moduli of about 1.4 kilopascals for grey matter and 1.9 for white matter in cow brain , and in human tissue the best-fitting models give a shear modulus (how easily it deforms when one layer slides over another) of about 0.4 to 1.4 kilopascals . Those numbers are hard to feel, so here is an image rather than a measurement: the comparison usually made is to soft tofu or a set jelly. It holds its shape on a plate, and it tears if you pull on it. Mechanically, it is “nonlinear and viscoelastic” , which means it behaves partly like a spring and partly like honey, and stiffens the more you deform it.

That soft object does not sit directly against bone. It floats in cerebrospinal fluid, a thin layer of clear liquid that fills the space between brain and skull, and it is tethered at the bottom by the brainstem and loosely by membranes and blood vessels. The skull around it is hard and, on the outside, smooth. The inside of its floor is not. The front of the brain rests on the bony roofs of the eye sockets, and the tips of the temporal lobes sit in two cup-shaped hollows on either side, behind a sharp ledge of bone called the sphenoid ridge. As Bigler puts it, “these concavities of the skull base cup the frontal and temporal lobes”, and the ridge and the edge of the tentorium (a stiff fold of membrane that separates the back of the brain from the cerebellum) “are uniquely situated to facilitate injury to the posterior base of the frontal lobe and the anterior pole and medial surface area of the temporal lobe” . Keep those two places in mind: the underside of the frontal lobes and the front tips of the temporal lobes.

The model below is a real brain surface, reconstructed from MRI, inside a skull. Turn it, open the skull, and pick a region to see where it is and what it does.

The functions in that model are summaries, and the brain does not really divide its work this neatly, but the broad strokes matter for this series. The frontal lobes, and in particular their underside (the orbitofrontal cortex), are heavily involved in planning, holding back impulses and regulating emotion. The temporal lobes hold the machinery for forming new memories and for processing emotion. These are the regions that sit on the rough parts of the skull floor. If you were designing a skull to protect personality, mood and memory, you would not put them there.

What a blow does

Now strike the box. The skull is pushed one way, and for a brief moment the brain, which is only loosely attached and has inertia of its own, stays where it was. The skull’s inner wall catches up with the brain on the side that was struck and compresses it there, and when the skull is stopped (by the neck, or by the floor) the brain carries on moving and meets the far wall. Neuropathologists call the bruise at the site of the blow a coup injury and the bruise on the opposite side a contrecoup injury. The textbook chapter on neuropathology describes the mechanism of most non-penetrating injury as “rapid acceleration or deceleration of the head, with or without impact” . “With or without impact” is the important part. What hurts the brain is the motion, and the skull does not need to break for that to happen.

Below is a deliberately crude model of the idea: a soft body in a fluid inside a rigid shell, with a ridged floor at the front. It is not a brain and not a simulation of one, but it obeys the same basic rule, which is that a soft, loosely held thing lags behind its container.

Try the blow to the forehead and the fall backwards a few times each. In both, the front of the body ends up hitting the front of the shell, once as the coup and once as the contrecoup. In a real head the front of the brain also rests on the ridged floor, so every time it is thrown forwards or back it scrapes across bone as well. That is the intuition behind a pattern that surprises most people, which is that contusions cluster in the frontal and temporal poles more or less regardless of where on the head the blow lands . The skull floor is shaped so that whatever the brain does in those first milliseconds, its front and its temporal tips grind against something rough.

The 3D model can do the same thing on real anatomy. Choose where the blow comes from and how hard, and press Strike.

When the head turns

Bruises on the surface are only half of the story, and for mild injury probably the smaller half. In 1943 the physicist A. H. S. Holbourn, reasoning from physical models of the head, argued that brain tissue is very hard to compress but very easy to shear, and that it is therefore rotation of the head, more than straight-line acceleration, that damages it . Think of the jelly again. Push it straight and it moves as a block; twist the plate quickly and the edge goes with the plate while the middle lags behind, and the jelly in between is stretched. Ommaya and Gennarelli later tied this idea to concussion and loss of consciousness, proposing that as the severity of rotation rises, the shearing reaches progressively deeper structures .

The experimental evidence for this is from monkeys, and it is not pleasant to read, but it is clear. In 1982 Gennarelli and colleagues accelerated the heads of 45 primates without any impact at all, varying only the direction of the rotation . Brief coma of under 15 minutes (a concussion) followed in 11 of 13 animals rotated front to back, 2 of 6 rotated obliquely and 2 of 26 rotated sideways. All 15 concussed animals recovered and showed no diffuse axonal injury. But 20 of the animals rotated sideways were in coma for more than six hours, all were severely disabled, and their brains showed the axonal damage seen in severe human injury. The authors concluded that “axonal damage produced by coronal head acceleration is a major cause of prolonged traumatic coma and its sequelae” , and nothing had struck any of those skulls.

How hard is the motion in an ordinary concussion? The best numbers come from American football, because players can be filmed, reconstructed with crash-test dummies or fitted with sensors in their helmets.

A concussed professional player’s head, on average, briefly experienced about 98 times the acceleration of gravity, over about 15 milliseconds . What I find more telling is how much the ranges overlap. In the college study, concussive impacts ranged from about 61 g to about 169 g, and how severe the concussion was clinically had nothing to do with the size of the impact. The authors were candid that “it may be difficult to establish a threshold for concussive injury that can be applied to all football players” . The same blow can concuss one person and not the next, which is part of why concussion is so hard to see from the outside.

What the rotation does inside is easiest to picture with the brain’s wiring. Nerve cells talk over long, thin cables called axons, bundled together in the white matter, and each axon is held in shape by an internal scaffold of protein tubes (microtubules) that also act as the rails along which the cell transports material. Axons are, in the words of one review, “especially vulnerable to injury due to the mechanical loading of the brain”, and diffuse axonal injury “has been found in all severities of TBI and may represent a key pathologic substrate of mild TBI (concussion)” .

In other words, the stretch lasts milliseconds but the damage plays out over a day, and in people, “axonal degeneration has been found to continue even years after injury” . Where it happens is also not random. In a classic study of 434 fatal non-penetrating head injuries, Adams and colleagues found diffuse axonal injury in 122, and graded it by where the damage reached: the white matter of the hemispheres, then a focal lesion in the corpus callosum (the thick band of fibres joining the two halves of the brain), then a lesion in the upper brainstem . In 24 of those cases the injury could only be seen under the microscope. The last model below shows the same idea in three dimensions, with the long fibre bundles drawn in.

None of the damage in this section needs a broken skull, a bleed, or anything that shows up on the CT scan used in most emergency departments. In one study of 135 people with mild TBI, 27% of those with a normal CT on admission had an abnormal MRI soon after, and contusions or four or more small bleeds along axons on that MRI predicted a worse outcome at three months . A normal CT, on its own, does not show that the brain was spared.

There is a way to see some of this damage in living people, though only on average, and it relies on water. Water molecules in the brain are always jiggling about at random, and in most tissue they wander as easily in one direction as another. Inside a bundle of axons that changes, because the membranes and the myelin wrapped around them make it far easier for water to drift along the fibres than across them. Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) measures that preference in every small cube of the brain , and summarises it as a number between 0 and 1 called fractional anisotropy, or FA: 0 if water spreads equally in every direction, and close to 1 if it spreads only along a line . By following the preferred direction from one cube to the next, you can trace the long bundles themselves. The figure below shows tracts traced this way through an average of 842 brains.

The intuition is that a damaged axon should leak, which would make diffusion less directional and FA lower, and in group studies that is broadly what turns up. A meta-analysis of thirteen studies found lower FA in the corpus callosum of people with mild TBI than in controls, most clearly in its back end, the splenium . A tally of the wider literature found the frontal tracts reported most often, the corona radiata and the front of the corpus callosum among them . Then again, the differences are small, and they shift with time: some studies in the first two weeks find FA higher than normal, and later studies mostly find it lower . This is also how a CT can be normal while DTI is not, because CT is very good at showing blood and broken bone, and a stretched axon contains neither.

All of this describes groups, and I want to be plain about that. In the TRACK-TBI study, patients whose CT and MRI were clear showed no significant DTI difference from controls as a group , and the radiologists’ review of the evidence concluded that DTI belongs, for now, to research comparisons, and cannot yet tell whether one particular person’s white matter was injured . What the figure can do is show where in the wiring group studies have looked and found differences.

The second injury

So far everything I have described happens in the first fraction of a second. The neuroscientists who study concussion call this the primary injury, and it is, in one review’s words, “the direct mechanical damage”, which “cannot be therapeutically influenced” . By the time anyone could treat it, it is over. What follows over the next hours, days and weeks is the secondary injury, and that is where medicine has tried to intervene. The textbook chapter on epidemiology puts it bluntly: “there is no effective treatment to reverse the effects of the primary brain injury sustained, and treatment is aimed at minimising the secondary brain injury that can occur due to the effects of ischaemia, hypoxia and raised intracranial pressure” .

Giza and Hovda pulled together decades of animal work into what they called the neurometabolic cascade of concussion . It is worth walking through slowly, because it explains why a brain that looks fine can be, for a while, unusually fragile.

The sequence, roughly, is this. The mechanical stretch pokes holes in cell membranes, so that potassium floods out of nerve cells and sodium and calcium flood in, and the cells release glutamate, a signalling chemical, “hyperacute” and “indiscriminate” . Every cell then tries to pump the ions back where they belong, and the pumps run on energy, so “ATP-requiring membrane ionic pumps shift into overdrive, causing hyperglycolysis” (a burst of glucose burning) and a “relative depletion of intracellular energy reserves” . The calcium that got in is mopped up by mitochondria, the cell’s power stations, which impairs them. After the burst comes a long slump: glucose metabolism falls into “a state of impaired metabolism that can last up to 7-10 days in adult animals” . Calcium inside axons also collapses their internal scaffolding, which links the cascade back to the axon figure above.

There is a practical consequence that I think everyone who plays a contact sport should know about. During that slump the brain is more vulnerable to a second injury. Clinically the window of greatest vulnerability looks like the first ten days, and in animal models two injuries three to five days apart did more damage than two injuries seven days apart . Inflammation adds another layer over the following days and weeks, and it has been linked to later neurodegeneration .

Why there is no drug

If the secondary injury unfolds over days, you would think it should be possible to interrupt it. People have been trying for a long time. The abstract of our BMC Neurology paper says it flatly: “no drug exists to prevent the spread of secondary injuries after a primary impact” . That sentence is backed by an unusual amount of failure.

A review of the field in 2010 counted 33 large phase III trials in TBI between 1980 and 2009, and said that their “disappointing results … have led to a critical reappraisal of clinical trial methodology” . Steroids, which reduce swelling elsewhere in the body, made things worse: in the CRASH trial of more than ten thousand adults, more people died within two weeks on steroids than on placebo . Progesterone failed in two large trials. ProTECT III was stopped for futility after 882 of a planned 1,140 patients , and in SyNAPSe the progesterone and placebo groups had favourable outcomes 50.4% and 50.5% of the time . Donald Stein, who had championed progesterone, wrote afterwards that “a 100% failure rate continues to plague the field of TBI trials” . A systematic review of 191 completed trials of acute care concluded that “considerable investment of resources … has resulted in very little translatable evidence” . Anti-inflammatory drugs have also failed in trials , and Dr Sudhakar’s own review of drugs that act on the brain’s main inhibitory signalling system found that in animal models they “fail to produce any neuroprotection after a primary impact to the brain” and can be harmful .

I should be precise about the claim, because it is easy to overstate. There are treatments that help people with TBI: neurosurgery, intensive care that keeps oxygen and blood pressure up and pressure inside the skull down, and rehabilitation. And one drug did reduce deaths in a large trial. Tranexamic acid, which stops bleeding rather than protecting nerve cells, reduced head-injury deaths in people with mild to moderate TBI when given within three hours, though not in severe TBI . What has not worked, so far, is a drug that protects the brain’s cells from the secondary cascade itself. Why is a question the field argues about, and I am not in a position to settle it. Many of the explanations offered come back to the same thing, though, which is that TBI is not one disease: the mix of bruising, bleeding, axonal damage and swelling differs from one person to the next, and so does what comes after. Which brings me to how we decide who has a mild injury and who has a severe one.

Counting consciousness

The most widely used measure of how badly a brain is injured is the Glasgow Coma Scale, published by Graham Teasdale and Bryan Jennett in 1974 . It asks three questions of a person who may not be able to answer you, and scores each: how readily do their eyes open, how well can they talk, and how well can they move on command. The three scores add up to a total between 3 and 15. My project, and both of the papers, describe sorting people by the total score recorded at admission into mild (13 to 15), moderate (9 to 12) and severe (3 to 8) . Try it.

Play with it for a minute and something odd shows up. A person who opens their eyes only when spoken to, is confused, and obeys commands scores 3 + 4 + 6 = 13: mild. A person who opens their eyes spontaneously, is orientated, but can only localise to pressure instead of obeying scores 4 + 5 + 5 = 14: also mild, and milder. Very different people can land on the same total. Teasdale himself, revisiting the scale forty years on, wrote that “individual patients are best described by the three components of the coma scale; whereas the derived total coma score should be used to characterise groups”, and that predicting outcome needs other information as well . That is a caveat that applies to my own work, which sorted people by a single total taken at admission.

Mild is not minor

Here is the part of the story that I most want readers to take away. “Mild” in “mild TBI” describes the score in the first hours, not the consequences. The textbook chapter on mild injury says that “for a sizeable minority of patients diagnosed with mTBI, the term can seem a cruel misnomer”, and that although most people’s symptoms (fatigue, irritability, poor concentration, headache, dizziness, sensitivity to noise and light, depression and anxiety) subside within three months, “in up to 30% of patients with mTBI, they can persist well beyond 6 months” .

Large studies since then have found it to be worse than that. TRACK-TBI followed 1,154 people with mild TBI from eleven US trauma centres, alongside 299 people with orthopaedic injuries (a broken leg, say) as a comparison . The outcome measure is the Glasgow Outcome Scale–Extended, whose top score (8) means a full return to the life a person had before; anything below 8 means some injury-related limitation, at work, at home or socially.

At two weeks, 87% of the people with mild TBI in TRACK-TBI reported some functional limitation. At twelve months it was still 53%, against 38% of the orthopaedic patients, and the authors concluded that “most patients with mTBI presenting to US level I trauma centers report persistent, injury-related life difficulties at 1 year postinjury” . That comparison group matters, because it answers the obvious objection: being injured badly enough to go to a trauma centre is disruptive whatever the injury, and some of that 53% would be there for reasons unrelated to the brain. The excess over the orthopaedic group is the part that is harder to explain away. The same study found that at three and six months about a fifth of the mild TBI group had probable post-traumatic stress disorder or major depression, against roughly a tenth of the orthopaedic group . In Europe, CENTER-TBI found that 30% of people sent home from the emergency department had not fully recovered at six months , and the Commission summarises the European and American studies together as showing that “the persisting effects of mild TBI are common and well outside the conventional perception of mild” .

Those are the people most likely to be told they are fine and sent home, and the Commission’s report notes how little follows: in CENTER-TBI only 26% were given written information and 6% a follow-up appointment, and 90% of centres do not routinely schedule follow-up after discharge from the emergency department . The papers my project produced quote an old description of mild TBI as a “silent epidemic”, “because the sign and symptoms of the injury don’t usually manifest immediately leading to difficulties in diagnosis” . The other side of the blunt labels is worth stating too: in TRACK-TBI, by twelve months 52.4% of people with severe TBI and 75% of those with moderate TBI had a favourable outcome . The severity label given at admission is a rough guide to what follows, in both directions.

A process, not an event

In 2010 Brent Masel and Douglas DeWitt published a paper whose title is the argument: “Traumatic brain injury: a disease process, not an event” . They argued that TBI “is a chronic disease process, one that fits the World Health Organization definition”, that it “increases long-term mortality and reduces life expectancy”, and that it is associated with seizures, sleep disorders, neurodegenerative diseases, hormonal problems and psychiatric illness, as well as conditions well outside the brain such as metabolic dysregulation. They were careful to add that their “intent is not to discourage patients with TBI or their families and caregivers, but rather to emphasize that TBI should be managed as a chronic disease” . Corrigan and Hammond made the same case from rehabilitation, describing brain injuries as “dynamic conditions that continue to change years after onset” , and a Lancet Neurology review found that outcomes can improve or worsen “up to two decades after injury” . Between one and five years after injury, according to the Commission, “decline occurs as frequently as improvement” .

The figure below lays some of the evidence along a timeline. It is not one person’s story, and the studies do not all look at the same people, but together they give a sense of how long the tail is.

A few of these deserve a sentence each. In a study of 2.79 million Danes, people with any TBI had about 1.24 times the risk of dementia of people without one, rising with the number of injuries, and the excess was largest in the first six months . In 7.4 million Danes, the suicide rate was about twice as high after TBI, and still about 1.8 times as high after mild TBI alone . And in a US study that matched 4,351 people with mild TBI to 4,351 unexposed people and followed them for up to ten years, mild TBI was associated with about 2.5 times the risk of developing high blood pressure, 1.9 times the risk of diabetes and 2.2 times the risk of ischaemic stroke or transient ischaemic attack (a “mini-stroke”), with new conditions appearing at a median of three and a half years after injury . In people aged 18 to 40 with mild TBI, the hazard ratio for high blood pressure was 5.9. The authors called for “a targeted screening program for multisystem diseases after TBI” . For the people in the US database I used, who had more severe injuries on average, life expectancy was about nine years shorter than for comparable people in the general population .

Some of these associations will be causal and some will not. People who fall over are not a random sample of people, and neither are people who crash motorbikes; conditions that were already there can make an injury more likely, and the same habits or circumstances can raise the risk of both. Most of these studies adjust for what they can, and none of them can adjust for everything. I come back to this in Part 3, because it applies just as much to my own work.

Illnesses that travel together

The word for what that timeline is circling is comorbidity, and since the rest of the series hangs on it, I want to pin it down. Comorbidity means two or more conditions in the same person, whether at the same time or one after the other. It says nothing, by itself, about why. Two neighbouring words do carry a claim about cause, and it helps to keep them apart. A complication is something the injury or its treatment directly brings about, usually soon after (a seizure in the first week, an infection in hospital). A sequela is a lasting consequence of the injury (memory problems from a damaged temporal lobe). Comorbidity is the broader, more agnostic term, and it is the honest one for the kind of data my project used, because a survey that records which conditions a person has can tell you that two things go together without telling you how.

So why do conditions go together? This was the question I found most interesting in the project, and also the one my data could answer least. There are at least six routes, and they leave very similar footprints in data.

The first route is plain chance. If high blood pressure affects a lot of older people and so do cataracts, plenty of people will have both without either having anything to do with the other, and a common condition will turn up alongside almost everything. The second is the one people usually assume: one condition causes the other, as when chronic pain wears a person down into depression. The third is a shared mechanism, a single underlying process that produces both, as when the same damage to frontal and limbic circuits could make someone both more anxious and more prone to low mood. The fourth is a shared risk factor, sometimes called a confounder: age raises the risk of high blood pressure, high cholesterol, cataracts and osteoarthritis all at once, and alcohol, poverty or a dangerous job can do the same for other sets of conditions. The fifth is treatment, where a medicine for one condition brings on another. The sixth is detection: a person who is already under a doctor’s care for one condition gets examined, asked about and diagnosed more, so conditions look more connected among patients than they are in life. My project could not tell these apart, and I say so again in Part 3, but knowing they exist changes how you read every line in a comorbidity network.

With that in hand, here is what is known, and what is suspected, about the conditions that follow a brain injury, family by family.

Psychiatric

Anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress disorder were among the five commonest new conditions five years after a mild TBI in the database I used, with panic attacks not far behind , and probable PTSD or major depression was more than twice as common after mild TBI as after an orthopaedic injury at three months, and still more common at six . Two routes are usually proposed and probably both operate: damage to the frontal and temporal regions that regulate emotion , and the disruption to work, money and relationships that any serious injury brings.

Substance use

Here the arrow often points the other way. Alcohol is involved in 15 to 20% of TBIs in India and was a contributing factor for a quarter of patients in CENTER-TBI , so drinking is as much a cause of injury as a consequence, which is the shared-risk-factor route in action. Accidental poisoning is among the causes of death with the highest excess risk after TBI .

Heart, blood vessels and metabolism

After mild TBI, high blood pressure, diabetes and stroke (or transient ischaemic attack) all became more likely over the following decade, even in people aged 18 to 40 . Why is not settled. Masel and DeWitt list neuroendocrine and systemic metabolic dysregulation among TBI’s long-term effects ; reduced activity, sleep problems and stress are other plausible contributors, and I would treat all of these as proposed routes rather than established ones.

Hormones

The hypothalamus and pituitary, which run most of the body’s hormone systems, sit at the base of the brain just above the skull floor described earlier, and neuroendocrine dysregulation is one of the long-term consequences Masel and DeWitt name . Injury to that region is the usual proposed route.

Neurological

Seizures, sleep disorders and neurodegenerative disease are all associated with TBI , and TBI is a risk factor for epilepsy, stroke and neurodegeneration . The dementia risk rises with the number of injuries , and continuing axonal degeneration is one proposed link .

Pain and the body

Chronic pain was as common as depression five years after mild TBI , and back pain topped the list ten years after moderate and severe TBI . The accident that injures the brain often injures the rest of the body too, which is the most direct route of all, and age adds osteoarthritis on top.

None of these families sits in isolation, and it is easy to imagine how they might feed one another: pain disturbing sleep, poor sleep lowering mood, low mood making it harder to stay active, inactivity raising blood pressure, and so on around a circle. Each of those links is plausible, and some are well studied in other settings, but nothing in this post shows that they operate after TBI. Still, the possibility of a circle like that is the best reason I can give for looking at these conditions as a network rather than as a list.

Tangles

This is where my project begins. The first paper that came out of it asked a simple question of the TBI Model Systems (TBIMS) database, which is the largest longitudinal TBI dataset in the world and has followed some participants for 35 years : five years after a mild TBI, how many people have been diagnosed with each of 26 medical and psychiatric conditions since their injury ? Of the 10,564 people in the database whose admission GCS was recorded, the paper counted 4,915 (46.5%) in the mild range. A caveat that runs through the whole series is that these are not typical concussions. Everyone in TBIMS was admitted for inpatient rehabilitation, which fewer than one in ten hospitalised TBI patients receives , and the mild cases there were “typically characterized by the presence of intracranial pathology and/or PTA” (post-traumatic amnesia, a stretch of time after the injury the person cannot remember) . Only 223 to 228 of them answered the questions about other conditions at the five-year follow-up, for a reason Part 3 explains.

Of the 26, ten stand out by how common they were.

Anxiety (16.1%), depression (15.7%), chronic pain (15.7%), high blood pressure (14.0%) and post-traumatic stress disorder (11.2%) top the list . The younger people (50 or under at the follow-up) had more depression than the older ones, and the older ones more high blood pressure, high cholesterol, cataracts and osteoarthritis, which is roughly what you would expect from age alone; post-traumatic stress disorder was more common in women. The paper concluded that “individuals who have sustained mild TBI could develop serious long-term medical and psychiatric comorbidities which could affect their pace of recovery” , and it said nothing about cause, deliberately.

A list of percentages, though, treats each condition as if it lived alone, and the previous section was about why that is wrong. Someone with depression after a brain injury is also more likely to have anxiety, panic attacks and trouble sleeping, and the press of a button above shows that those overlaps are not small. Once you start drawing the lines, the list turns into a tangle, and the question my capstone was really about is how you see the structure of a tangle like that. Which conditions sit at the centre, which ones bridge otherwise separate groups, and does the shape of the tangle change with age? Could a condition that is rare be important because of where it sits, rather than how often it occurs? And if it could, what would a doctor do differently with that knowledge?

Answering those questions needs a way of thinking about connections that most people (and I, at the start of the project) have never been taught. That is what Part 2 is for.

Part 1The quiet injury Part 2Thinking in graphs Part 3A map of what comes after

About the 3D brain: the cortex is FreeSurfer’s fsaverage surface (Fischl et al. 1999), parcellated with the Destrieux atlas (Destrieux et al. 2010); deep structures come from the Harvard-Oxford and Juelich atlases in MNI152 space, processed with nilearn (Abraham et al. 2014). The skull and fibre bundles are derived or stylised, and the mechanics are a toy model. Sources and build steps are in the repository’s assets/data/tbi/README.md.
entry.summary: Part 1 of a series on traumatic brain injury. What a brain injury is, how a blow that never breaks the skull can still damage a brain, why “mild” is a misleading word, and why the injury is better thought of as the start of a long process than as an event.

entry.title: Thinking in graphs
entry.content:
In 1735 Leonhard Euler settled a question about the bridges of a Prussian city by throwing away almost everything there was to know about the city.
Part 1The quiet injury Part 2Thinking in graphs Part 3A map of what comes after

How do you look at a tangle?

Part 1 ended with the conditions that turn up in the years after a mild traumatic brain injury. Think of one person five years on. The injury itself may be long healed in the sense that a scan would show nothing, but they are more likely than they would otherwise have been to be living with depression, or anxiety, or trouble sleeping, or chronic pain, or high blood pressure, and quite often with several of these at once. For a clinician seeing that person, this is a list of problems to manage. For anyone trying to understand what a brain injury does to people in general, though, it is something messier: thousands of people, each carrying a different handful of conditions, with the handfuls overlapping in ways that are hard to hold in your head. It is a tangle, and the question this post is about is how you look at one.

The answer I used in my undergraduate capstone at Krea University, supervised by Dr Shyam Kumar Sudhakar, and in the papers that came out of it , was graph theory. I had not met it formally before that project, and most of what follows is what I wish someone had shown me at the start. I want to build it up from nothing, with figures you can push around, because I think the ideas are much simpler than their notation suggests, and because almost all of them come from a person asking a plain question about who is connected to whom. If you already know the definitions, I hope the figures still give you a slightly different angle on them.

There is one move that runs through the whole series, and it is worth naming before the first figure. It is the act of recasting: taking a problem that looks like it is about one thing (a city, a group of friends, a population of patients) and deciding that the only thing that matters about it is what is connected to what. Everything else gets thrown away. That sounds like a loss, and sometimes it is, but it is also what lets a single set of tools work on bridges, friendships, power grids, brains and diseases.

Seven bridges

Königsberg (now Kaliningrad) was built where the river Pregel splits around two islands. Seven bridges joined the islands and the two banks, and the story goes that people liked to ask whether you could take a walk through the city that crossed every bridge exactly once. Try it.

You will have got stuck, and so does everyone, but getting stuck six times does not prove that the seventh attempt will fail. Euler’s contribution was to show that it must. His first step was to notice that nearly everything about the city is irrelevant. The shape of the islands, the length of the bridges, the streets you walk along on the way, none of it changes the answer. All that matters is which land masses are joined by how many bridges. That is the recasting, and the second half of the figure shows it: each land mass becomes a dot and each bridge a line.

The second step is an argument about counting, and it is short enough to follow in full. Think about any land mass that is neither where your walk starts nor where it ends. Every time you arrive there by one bridge you have to leave by another, so the bridges you use there come in pairs, and if you are to use all of them, that land mass must touch an even number of bridges. Only the start and the end can be odd. In Königsberg, Kneiphof touches five bridges and each of the other three land masses touches three, which makes four odd land masses, and a walk can have at most two ends. No route exists, and no amount of trying will find one.

Building a bridge in the figure lets you check the converse. Make every land mass even, and a walk exists that can even end where it began; make exactly two odd, and a walk exists that must start at one of them and end at the other. Euler stated this, though the proof that the condition is enough, as well as necessary, came from Carl Hierholzer in 1873 , and the “Find a walk” button uses his method. The city itself has since changed the puzzle. Its bridges have been added, destroyed and rebuilt over the centuries, so that the walk has been possible in some periods and impossible in others, and after one of them was rebuilt in 2005 the chemist Roger Mallion went to Kaliningrad and walked an Eulerian route in February 2006 .

I should be honest about one part of the story as it is usually told. Euler did not draw the dots-and-lines picture. His paper, presented to the St Petersburg Academy in 1735 and published in 1741, reasons with letters for the regions and the bridges, and the diagrams we now call graphs only appear in the second half of the nineteenth century . The drawing came later; the idea that only the connections matter is Euler’s.

Dots and lines

So here is the object itself. A graph $G = (V, E)$ is a set of nodes (or vertices) $V$ and a set of edges $E$, where each edge joins two nodes. That is the whole definition. A graph is a guest list together with a list of who knows whom; it says nothing about where anyone is standing.

Two refinements matter for this series. An edge can carry a weight, a number saying how strong the connection is, which makes the graph weighted. And an edge can have a direction, from one node to another, as a follow on social media does, which makes the graph directed. The disease networks in Part 3 are weighted and undirected. They are weighted because some pairs of conditions are much more strongly associated than others. They are undirected because the study can only see that two conditions turn up together in the same people, and co-occurrence is not causation: depression and chronic pain appearing together tells you nothing on its own about which, if either, led to the other. An arrow would claim something the data cannot support.

The matrix on the right is called the adjacency matrix, $A$, and it is the same information as the drawing in a different form: $a_{ij} = 1$ if nodes $i$ and $j$ are joined and $0$ if not, or the weight of the edge in a weighted graph. Computers work with the matrix, which is why most of the formulas below are written in terms of $a_{ij}$. People work with the drawing, and the drawing has a trap in it.

Drag a few people around, or press “Redraw the picture”. The matrix does not change, because the graph has not changed. A drawing of a graph is one of infinitely many, and where a node sits on the page carries no information unless someone has decided that it should. This is easy to forget when reading network figures. When a network figure in a paper puts two nodes close together, it is tempting to read closeness as similarity, and sometimes the layout algorithm has made that roughly true; but the data is the list of edges, and everything else is a choice made to help the eye. The tangle at the top of the post is the extreme case. I will keep coming back to the question of what a picture can and cannot tell you, because it matters a great deal once the nodes are diseases.

Who has the most friends?

The first question anyone asks about a network is who has the most connections. The degree of a node $u$ is the number of edges touching it,

\[k_u = \sum_{v} a_{uv},\]

which is just the row sum of the adjacency matrix. In a weighted graph there is a second answer: the weighted degree, or strength, adds up the weights instead of counting the edges,

\[s_u = \sum_{v} w_{uv},\]

where $w_{uv}$ is the weight of the edge between $u$ and $v$ (zero if there is none). The two can disagree, and the difference between them is worth noticing.

Ravi has the most friends, but they are all acquaintances; Mina has fewer, and they are close. Neither number is the right one in general, and which you want depends on the question. If you want to know who hears gossip from the most directions, count. If you want to know whose absence would be felt most, weigh. In a comorbidity network the weights are measures of how strongly two conditions are associated, so a condition with a high degree is associated with many others, and a condition with a high weighted degree has strong associations, which need not be the same conditions at all.

The third button shows something that surprises most people. Scott Feld pointed out in 1991 that most people have fewer friends than their friends do, on average , and in this little network it is true of most of the ten. It sounds like a statement about popularity and self-esteem, though it follows from arithmetic alone. A person with many friends appears in many friends’ lists, so when you average over friends you count the popular people again and again. Averaging over edges rather than over people gives $\langle k^2 \rangle / \langle k \rangle$, which is never less than the ordinary mean $\langle k \rangle$ and is larger whenever degrees vary at all. The same bias applies to anything sampled by following edges. If you find patients by asking a patient to name others, or meet conditions by following them from a condition you already know, you will meet the well-connected ones first.

How much could be connected, and is?

The next question is about the network as a whole: how full is it? Among $V$ nodes there are $V(V-1)/2$ possible pairs, and the density is the share of them that are actually joined,

\[\text{density} = \frac{2E}{V(V-1)},\]

where $E$ is the number of edges. The factor of 2 is there because each edge is one of the $V(V-1)/2$ pairs.

I think of the faint lines as ghosts, the friendships that could exist and don’t. Density is the fraction of ghosts that have become real. Adding nodes without adding edges makes a network sparser very quickly, because the number of possible pairs grows with the square of the number of nodes. Most real networks are very sparse for exactly this reason: no one can know everyone in a city. A disease network has only a couple of dozen nodes, so its density can be much higher, and in Part 3 the interesting question will be less “how dense is it?” than “which of the ghosts became real, and why those?”

How far apart is everyone?

Two nodes that are not joined directly may still be joined through others. The distance $\delta(v_i, v_j)$ between them is the number of edges on the shortest path from one to the other. Finding it is easier than it sounds, and the method, breadth-first search, has a lovely physical picture. Drop a stone into a pond at the starting node: the first ripple reaches its neighbours, the second reaches their neighbours, and so on, and the ripple that first touches a node tells you how far away it is.

Two numbers summarise all the distances in a connected network. The average path length is the mean over every pair,

\[\bar{\delta} = \frac{2}{V(V-1)} \sum_{i \lt j} \delta(v_i, v_j),\]

and the diameter is the largest distance between any pair, $D = \max_{i,j} \delta(v_i, v_j)$: the furthest apart two nodes can be. In the histogram the average is the dashed line and the diameter is the right-most bar.

Now press “Add a shortcut”. A single edge between far corners pulls the whole histogram to the left and cuts the average by a surprising amount, because it shortens not one journey but every journey that can use it. Hold on to that, because it is the heart of the small-world idea later on.

The most famous measurement of a path length was made with letters.
