In the 1960s Stanley Milgram and Jeffrey Travers asked 296 people in Nebraska and Boston to get a document to a stockbroker in Massachusetts by passing it only to someone they knew on first-name terms. Sixty-four of the chains arrived, and those took an average of 5.2 intermediaries , which is where “six degrees of separation” comes from (a phrase the paper did not use, and an average over the chains that finished, which were probably the shorter ones). In 2012 a team at Facebook and the University of Milan reported the same quantity computed directly for all of Facebook’s roughly 721 million active users, and the average distance came out at 4.74 .

For diseases, a short path between two conditions would mean they are linked through a few intermediate conditions that each co-occur with the next. I want to be careful here, because it is very easy to read a path as a mechanism, as if one condition led to the next and then the next. In an undirected co-occurrence network a path is only a chain of associations. It suggests where to look; it does not show what happens.

Are my friends friends with each other?

Pick a person and look only at their friends. Do those friends know each other? In some circles nearly everyone does, and in others the person is the only thing the friends have in common. The clustering coefficient of a node $u$ measures this. If $u$ has $k_u$ neighbours, they could share $k_u(k_u-1)/2$ edges among themselves; if $E_u$ of those exist, then

\[C_u = \frac{2E_u}{k_u(k_u-1)}, \qquad 0 \le C_u \le 1.\]

Every edge between two of $u$’s neighbours closes a triangle through $u$, so $E_u$ is also the number of triangles that $u$ sits in. The network’s average clustering is the mean of $C_u$ over all nodes, $\bar{C} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_u C_u$.

Clustering is density again, but local: it is the density of the little network formed by one node’s neighbours. That is why it says something different from the global density. A network can be sparse overall and still be made of tight knots, and social networks usually are, because friends introduce their friends to each other. One detail matters for reading the numbers in Part 3: a node with fewer than two neighbours has no pairs to close, and conventions differ on what to do with it. networkx, the Python library the analysis used, gives it $C_u = 0$ and still includes it in the average , so a few dangling nodes pull the average down; Gephi, a widely used program for drawing networks, leaves such nodes out. For the network in my thesis the two conventions give 0.38 and 0.42, and the 0.42 the thesis reported is the second kind.

In a disease network, a triangle is three conditions where each pair co-occurs more than chance would predict. A condition with many triangles sits inside a knot of conditions that tend to come together. Whether that knot reflects a shared cause, a shared treatment, a shared way of being diagnosed, or something else entirely is not something the triangle can tell you, but it is a good place to start asking.

Do hubs hold hands?

Once you know some nodes have many connections and some few, a natural question is who connects to whom. Do the well-connected nodes link to each other, or do they mostly link to the poorly connected ones? This is degree assortativity, and Mark Newman’s way of measuring it is direct . Take every edge, write down the degree at each end, and compute the ordinary correlation between the two columns:

\[r = \frac{\sum_{e} j_e k_e / M - \left[ \sum_{e} \tfrac{1}{2}(j_e + k_e) / M \right]^2}{\sum_{e} \tfrac{1}{2}(j_e^2 + k_e^2) / M - \left[ \sum_{e} \tfrac{1}{2}(j_e + k_e) / M \right]^2},\]

where the sums run over the $M$ edges and $j_e$, $k_e$ are the degrees of the two nodes that edge $e$ joins. It looks heavy, but it is nothing more than a Pearson correlation coefficient, and it runs from $-1$ to $+1$. Positive means hubs attach to hubs; negative means hubs attach to the periphery. My thesis wrote it in the language networkx uses, comparing the joint distribution of degrees at the two ends of an edge with what independence would give, $P(k_i, k_j) = P(k_i)P(k_j)$; it comes to the same number.

The rewiring in the figure is the important part, because it shows that assortativity is a property of the wiring and not of the degrees. Every node keeps exactly the number of edges it started with, yet the network can be pushed from hubs that avoid each other to hubs that cling together, and the cloud of dots in the scatter plot tilts with it. When you push hard enough, the hubs fold into a dense core and the low-degree nodes are left to link among themselves in long strings.

Newman found that social networks tend to be assortative and technological and biological networks tend to be disassortative , and the marks under the figure show some of his values. One way to read the difference: in a network of collaborators, prolific people work with prolific people, whereas in the internet or a protein network, hubs are, in a sense, there to serve the periphery. For a disease network, positive assortativity would mean that conditions associated with many others tend to be associated with each other, forming a core of highly comorbid conditions, while the rarer, less connected conditions sit in their own corners. One caution I would give my undergraduate self: on a network of a couple of dozen nodes, this coefficient rests on few edges and can move a long way if a handful of them change.

Who matters?

“Which node is most important?” is the question people most want a network to answer, and it does not have one answer. It has several, each a different way of making “important” precise, and they are known collectively as centralities. My research used three.

Degree centrality is the simplest: a node matters if it has many connections. It is the degree, usually divided by $n-1$ so that a node connected to everyone scores 1. The thesis wrote it via the neighbourhood $N(u) = \lbrace v \in V : uv \in E \rbrace$, the set of nodes joined to $u$, whose size is the degree.

Betweenness centrality asks a different question: how much of the traffic in the network has to pass through this node? Picture everyone sending a message to everyone else along the shortest route available. A node that sits on many of those routes is a toll booth, a broker, a bridge between parts of the network that would otherwise have to go a long way round. Make a guess before anything is revealed.

Most people pick Hal or Rosa, because they are the obvious hubs, with six connections each. But Bea, with four, carries more than half of all the shortest paths between other pairs, because every journey from one side to the other has to go through her. Close her and the network falls into two islands. Hal and Rosa, for all their friends, are each only the centre of their own half.

Formally, if $\sigma_{uv}$ is the number of shortest paths between $u$ and $v$ and $\sigma_{uv}(w)$ is the number of those that pass through $w$, the betweenness of $w$ is

\[C_B(w) = \sum_{u \neq v \neq w} \frac{\sigma_{uv}(w)}{\sigma_{uv}},\]

so that each pair contributes the fraction of its shortest paths that $w$ lies on . Computing this naively means finding every shortest path between every pair; the trick that makes it fast, and that this page uses, is Ulrik Brandes’s 2001 algorithm, which runs one breadth-first search per node and accumulates the fractions on the way back .A note for anyone comparing numbers. The thesis writes the sum over $(u,v) \in V^2$, which counts each pair twice in an undirected graph. networkx sums over unordered pairs and, by default, divides by $(n-1)(n-2)/2$, the number of pairs not involving $w$, so that a value of 1 means $w$ is on every shortest path between every other pair (the centre of a star). The betweenness values in my thesis and papers, and in Part 3, are normalised this way. In this figure Bea’s 0.55 means that 55% of the pairs’ shortest-path traffic runs through her.

Milgram’s letters contain a real toll booth. Of the 64 chains that reached the stockbroker, 16 reached him through the same person, a clothing merchant in his home town, and two business associates accounted for another 15 between them . Half of all the successful chains funnelled through three people. In a disease network a high-betweenness condition is one that sits between groups of conditions that otherwise rarely meet. The papers made a point of this because betweenness did not simply track how common a condition was: some conditions were rare after mild TBI and yet sat on many of the network’s shortest paths. I will come back to what that might mean in Part 3.

Eigenvector centrality gives the third answer, and it is the hardest of the three to get a feel for. It says you are important if your neighbours are important. That sounds circular, and it is, but the circle can be solved. Give every node a score $x_v$ and ask that each score be proportional to the sum of its neighbours’ scores:

\[x_v = \frac{1}{\lambda} \sum_{t \in M(v)} x_t = \frac{1}{\lambda} \sum_{t \in V} a_{vt}\, x_t,\]

where $M(v)$ is the set of $v$’s neighbours and $\lambda$ is a constant. Written with the adjacency matrix, this is the eigenvector equation $A\mathbf{x} = \lambda \mathbf{x}$, and choosing the largest eigenvalue guarantees, for a connected network, a solution in which every score is positive . The way to find it is to stop solving and start iterating. Give everyone a score of 1, then let everyone pass their score to their neighbours, and repeat. I picture a drop of dye in water: it pools wherever the channels are densest, and after enough rounds the pattern stops changing.

After one round the scores are just degree plus one, and Pat leads easily. By the fourth round Quinn has overtaken Pat, because Quinn’s three friends are in the dense core and their scores keep growing, while Pat’s six friends know no one else and have nothing to pass back. Eigenvector centrality remembers who your friends are, and their friends, all the way out. The same idea, with some important modifications for direction and for pages that link nowhere, is at the heart of PageRank, the method Google was founded on . In a disease network a condition with high eigenvector centrality is associated with conditions that are themselves highly associated: it is embedded in the core. In the published version of my work, degree and eigenvector centrality turned out to be highly correlated across conditions, while betweenness told a different story , which is part of why the papers leaned on betweenness.

Small worlds

Two observations from earlier sections sit uneasily together. Social networks are full of triangles, with friends of friends being friends, which makes them locally dense and, you might think, slow to cross: a world of tight villages. Yet the average distance between two people is tiny. How can a network be both cliquish and small?

In 1998 Duncan Watts and Steven Strogatz answered this with a model simple enough to play with . Start with a ring of nodes, each joined to its nearest neighbours on either side. This is the village: lots of triangles, and a long way round to the other side. Now go through the edges and, with some probability $p$, cut one end loose and reattach it to a node chosen at random. At $p = 0$ you have the ring; at $p = 1$ you have a random network. The question is what happens in between.

The path length collapses long before the clustering does. A rewiring probability of a few in a hundred is enough to bring the average distance most of the way down to that of a random network, because each rewired edge is a shortcut like the one you added in the path-length figure, and shortcuts help everyone. But a few shortcuts barely disturb the triangles, so the network still looks like a village from the inside. That window, high clustering and short paths together, is what Watts and Strogatz called a small world, and they showed that real networks sat in it: the collaboration network of film actors, the power grid of the western United States and the nervous system of the worm C. elegans all had clustering far above that of a random network of the same size, with average path lengths only a little longer . The worldwide airline network is a later example. Its cities are on average 4.4 flights apart, yet its clustering is 0.62, against 0.049 for a randomised version of the same network .

That comparison against a random network of the same size is the part that matters, and my thesis did not make it. It described the TBI comorbidity network as having “a relatively small-world structure” on the strength of its clustering and its short average path. Rebuilding the analysis for this series, I made the comparison against 500 random networks with the same 25 nodes and 69 edges. The thesis network’s average clustering is 0.38 (0.42 by the convention the thesis used) against 0.23 for the random networks, and its average path length is 2.31 against 1.99. The clustering is well above chance; the short paths say less, because a network this dense has short paths almost however it is wired. So the claim holds, modestly. Part 3 makes the same comparison for the published network.

Islands

The last idea is about groups. Many networks are made of communities, sets of nodes much more densely connected to each other than to the rest, and finding them is one of the most common things people do with a network. One of the most intuitive methods, from Michelle Girvan and Mark Newman , uses betweenness backwards. The edges that link communities are the bridges, so they carry many shortest paths; remove the busiest edge, recompute, and repeat, and the network falls apart along its natural seams.

The study in Part 3 uses a cousin of this idea that removes the busiest nodes rather than edges, and then puts each removed node back into every group it touched, so that a condition can belong to more than one cluster. Part 3 steps through it.

One graph, many worlds

By now there are enough measures to see the real payoff of recasting. Once a problem is a graph, the same handful of numbers can be computed for it, but what they mean depends entirely on what the nodes and edges stand for. Below is one small network and four measures, and you can choose what it represents.

Some of the most striking uses of graphs in medicine have been exactly this kind of recasting. In 2007 Goh and colleagues built a “human disease network” from 1,284 disorders and 1,777 genes, joining two disorders whenever a gene was implicated in both . Nothing about that network required new data; it was a new way of looking at a catalogue that already existed, and it showed disorders clustering by shared genetic origin. Two years later Hidalgo and colleagues built a phenotypic disease network from the disease histories of more than 30 million patients, linking diseases that co-occurred in the same people, and found that patients tended to develop diseases close in the network to those they already had . That is very nearly the kind of network my research built for mild TBI, on a much smaller scale, and the field that grew around these ideas is now often called network medicine .

The recasting also works with people as the nodes. Christakis and Fowler followed a network of 12,067 people from the Framingham Heart Study over three decades and reported that a person’s chance of becoming obese rose by 57% if a friend became obese , a finding that started a long and useful argument about how much of that is contagion and how much is people choosing similar friends. Epidemics are the clearest case of all. On networks where a few nodes have enormous numbers of contacts, Pastor-Satorras and Vespignani showed that an infection need not cross any threshold of infectiousness to persist , which is a formal version of why super-spreaders matter. And the same structure that makes such networks robust to random failures makes them fragile to the targeted loss of their hubs , which is why it matters so much to know which nodes those are.

From people to diseases

Everything so far has been about networks where the nodes were obvious: people, airports, land masses. The research in Part 3 makes one more recasting, and it is the least obvious of all. The raw data is a table of people, each with a list of conditions they do or do not have. Nobody hands you a network. You have to decide that the conditions will be the nodes, and that two conditions are connected when they turn up together in the same people.

Add everyone and look at what you get. Depression ends up connected to almost everything, but that is partly because depression is the most common condition among these ten invented people; a common condition will co-occur with lots of others by chance alone. Counting shared people is therefore not quite the right weight for an edge. What you want to know is whether two conditions occur together more than you would expect if they had nothing to do with each other, and that is a question about the people who have neither as well as the people who have both, which is why Person 10, who adds nothing to the drawing, still matters. Part 3 answers it with a correlation coefficient for yes-or-no data and a significance test, and only draws an edge when the association is unlikely to be a coincidence.

Once that network exists, every measure in this post becomes a question about brain injury. What would a hub be: a condition so entangled with others that treating it might ease several more? What would a bridge be: a condition that links, say, mental health conditions to cardiovascular ones, so that it sits between two specialities that rarely talk? What would a triangle be: three conditions that keep company, and what might they share? Would the network be assortative, with the most comorbid conditions clinging together in a core? Would it look different for younger and older people? And how much of what we see would reflect the biology of an injured brain, rather than who gets diagnosed with what, and who stays in a study long enough to be asked?

Some of those questions the study could answer, and some it could not, and Part 3 tries to be clear about which are which.

entry.content:
Five years after a mild brain injury, 225 people answered a set of questions about their health. This is what their answers look like when you stop reading them as lists and start reading them as a network.
Part 1The quiet injury Part 2Thinking in graphs Part 3A map of what comes after

Where we left off

Part 1 was about the injury. A traumatic brain injury is damage to the brain from an outside force, and most of them are classed as mild, which is a statement about how responsive someone was when they arrived at hospital and not a promise about how the next ten years will go. The brain can be stretched and sheared without the skull breaking, the damage can keep unfolding for months and years after the impact, and there is still no drug that stops it. What follows, for many people, is a long tail of other conditions: depression, anxiety, sleep problems, chronic pain, high blood pressure, and often several of these at once .

Part 2 was about a way of looking. A graph is a set of things and the connections between them, and once a problem has been recast as one, a small set of measures (degree, path length, clustering, assortativity, betweenness, eigenvector centrality) lets you ask precise questions about its shape. It ended with a recasting that does not come naturally: taking a table of people and their conditions and turning it into a network in which the conditions are the nodes, joined when they turn up together in the same people more often than chance would allow.

This part is about the research that did that for mild traumatic brain injury (I will write TBI from here on). It began as my undergraduate capstone at Krea University in 2023, supervised by Dr Shyam Kumar Sudhakar , and grew into three papers with him: one measuring how common 26 conditions were five years after a mild TBI , a perspective arguing that comorbidity networks could be useful in TBI care , and one building the networks themselves, for everyone and separately for younger and older people . The question running through all of them is simple to state. After a mild TBI, which conditions keep company, and what does the web they form look like?

I want to walk through every step, from where the data comes from to what the final network can and cannot say, and to fill in enough of the surrounding medicine and statistics that each step makes sense on its own. For this post the whole analysis was also rebuilt from the raw public-use files and my original code, so every number in the figures below is either taken from the papers or recomputed from the same data.

Where the numbers come from

A database of people who went to rehab

The data comes from the Traumatic Brain Injury Model Systems (TBIMS) National Database. The TBIMS programme was set up in the United States in 1987 and is funded by the National Institute on Disability, Independent Living, and Rehabilitation Research. Its centres (currently 16) enrol people aged 16 or over who were admitted to hospital with a TBI and then received inpatient rehabilitation at one of them, and then follow them up by interview at one, two and five years after the injury and every five years after that, for decades in some cases . As of March 2022 it held information on 19,045 people , and it is often described as the largest longitudinal TBI dataset in the world . A de-identified public-use version is available on request, which is what an undergraduate with no clinical access could actually work with.

The most important thing to understand about TBIMS, for everything that follows, is who is in it. To be enrolled, a person had to be injured badly enough to be admitted to hospital and then to need inpatient rehabilitation, and the programme’s own materials note that people needing inpatient rehabilitation are fewer than one in ten of everyone hospitalised with a TBI . The “mild” injuries in this database are therefore not the typical concussion from a football tackle. The Frontiers paper described them as typically involving intracranial pathology or a period of post-traumatic amnesia (the mild group’s average amnesia lasted about ten days) . They are mild by one particular measure, which needs its own introduction.

What makes an injury “mild”

The Glasgow Coma Scale, described by Graham Teasdale and Bryan Jennett in 1974, scores how responsive someone is on three counts: whether and how they open their eyes (1 to 4), how they respond verbally (1 to 5), and how they move in response to instructions or pressure (1 to 6) . The three add up to a total between 3 and 15. By convention, 13 to 15 is mild, 9 to 12 moderate and 3 to 8 severe, and that is how the thesis and both papers describe the groups . It is worth knowing that the scale’s authors have since argued that individual patients are best described by the three components separately, and that the total is better used to characterise groups , which is what a study like this does.

In what follows, “mild” means mild as the papers define it.

From thousands to 225

The study did not use everyone with a mild injury. It used the five-year follow-up, chosen (as the thesis admitted plainly) somewhat arbitrarily, as a point far enough from the injury for the long tail to show . And at five years, it needed people who had answered a particular set of health questions.

Those questions, which the next section describes in detail, were about 26 long-term conditions, and only people who answered them can contribute to a network of those conditions.

The last step is the steep one. Of 1,915 people interviewed at five years, only 225 answered the health questions, because (as the rebuild made clear) the questions were only included in interviews conducted between 2017 and 2019. Most of the 225 were injured between about 2011 and 2014. The papers mention the small number, quoting 223 to 228 depending on the question , but not why it was small, and I think the reason matters: the 225 are not people who were especially willing to talk about their health, they are mostly the people whose five-year interview happened to fall in a three-year window.

The mild group as a whole is older than you might expect (a median age of 57 at injury) and mostly male, and falls are the commonest cause, followed by road traffic. That fits what is known about TBI in high-income countries, where falls in older people drive much of the burden . The 225 look much like the larger group they came from, which is reassuring, though it does not settle whether they differ in ways that these few variables cannot show.

Attrition is the quiet companion of every long study. People move, stop answering, become too unwell to take part, or die, and the ones who remain may not be like the ones who left. For a study of illness after injury, that is not a small worry: if the sickest people are the likeliest to drop out, the conditions we see at five years will understate what the injury does. I will come back to this.

What was asked, and how it became data

Part 1 introduced the conditions by family. Here I want to be exact about what each one is, what people were asked about it, and how an answer became a number, because every later step depends on it.

The 26 conditions

At each follow-up, the TBIMS interview includes a block of questions modelled on the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), asked in the style of “Has a doctor or other health professional ever told you that you have…?”. A condition counts only if a doctor or other health professional diagnosed it; self-diagnosis was not accepted . My thesis used 25 of these conditions (all but “other heart conditions”); the BMC paper used all 26 .

From answers to ones and zeros

In the data each condition is stored as a code: yes, no, or one of several codes for “unknown”, “refused” or “not asked”. Anything other than a clear yes or no is set aside, which is why the number of people behind each condition is a little below 225. One wrinkle, which I cannot fully resolve from the public files: the Frontiers paper notes that a condition reported at an earlier follow-up was not asked about again , so how earlier answers are carried forward to year five is something I would want to check before trusting any single person’s record.

So the data that goes into the network is, for each person and each condition, a 1 (diagnosed), a 0 (never diagnosed), or a blank. Everything from here on is arithmetic on those columns.

From people to pairs

The raw material, then, is 225 people, each with a yes or no for each of 26 conditions. To build a network we need to decide, for each of the $26 \times 25 / 2 = 325$ pairs of conditions, whether the two are connected and how strongly.

Four kinds of people

Take one pair, anxiety and depression. Every person who answered both questions falls into exactly one of four groups: they have both, they have anxiety but not depression, depression but not anxiety, or neither. Counting the four groups gives what statisticians call a two-by-two contingency table, and everything else in this section is a way of reading one.

Nineteen people have both anxiety and depression. Is that a lot? It depends on how common each condition is. If a third of people had anxiety and a third had depression, and the two had nothing to do with each other, you would still expect about a ninth of people to have both, simply by chance. So the question is never “how many have both?” but “how many have both, compared with what we would expect if the two were independent?” For anxiety and depression here, the expected number is about six, and nineteen is about three times that.

The second pair shows the other side. Depression and hypertension are both common in this group (each reported by about a third and a half of people, respectively, at any time), and 34 people have both. That looks like a strong overlap until you work out the expectation, which is also about 34. These two conditions are each common, and they meet exactly as often as two common conditions would if they never influenced each other at all. Counting shared people, as the toy network at the end of Part 2 did, would have drawn a thick edge between them; the comparison with chance draws none.

The phi coefficient

The measure the study used is the phi coefficient, $\varphi$, which is what you get if you code each condition as 1 (present) or 0 (absent) and compute the ordinary Pearson correlation between the two columns. Written in terms of the table, with $a$ people having both, $b$ only the first, $c$ only the second and $d$ neither,

\[\varphi = \frac{ad - bc}{\sqrt{(a+b)(c+d)(a+c)(b+d)}}.\]

The numerator is the heart of it. The product $ad$ grows when people tend to have both or neither (the two conditions agree), and $bc$ grows when people tend to have one without the other (they disagree). If the conditions are independent the two products balance, and $\varphi$ is zero. The denominator is the product of the four row and column totals, and it scales the result so that $\varphi$ runs from $-1$ (whenever one is present, the other is absent) to $+1$ (the two always occur together). For anxiety and depression, $\varphi = 0.48$, one of the strongest associations in the whole network and the value quoted in the BMC paper . For depression and hypertension it is 0.005. For cataracts and depression it is slightly negative, $-0.08$, with fewer people having both than chance would predict, plausibly because cataracts are a condition of older people and depression was reported more often by younger ones in this group.

Why not just compare with chance directly?

There is an obvious alternative to $\varphi$, and my thesis discussed it: divide the observed number with both by the number expected by chance. That ratio is called the relative risk (or observed-to-expected ratio) and it is perhaps the most intuitive measure of all; a relative risk of 3 means “three times as often as chance”. In 2009 César Hidalgo and colleagues built a disease network from the hospital records of more than 30 million elderly Americans and compared the two measures carefully. Their conclusion was that each is biased in its own way: relative risk “overestimates relationships involving rare diseases and underestimates the comorbidity between highly prevalent illnesses, whereas φ accurately discriminates comorbidities between pairs of diseases of similar prevalence but underestimates the comorbidity between rare and common diseases” . The figure below lets you see why.

With two rare conditions you can push the relative risk to 6 or more while $\varphi$ stays modest: a handful of shared cases is a large multiple of a tiny expectation, but it is still a handful of people. With two common conditions, the relative risk cannot climb far at all (if half of everyone has each, they cannot occur together more than twice as often as chance), while $\varphi$ can be large. And when one condition is rare and the other common, $\varphi$ is capped well below 1 however strongly they are linked. Neither measure is wrong; each answers a slightly different question. For a small sample with several rare conditions, $\varphi$ has the advantage of not producing dramatic-looking associations from three or four people, which is why the thesis chose it, but it is worth remembering that a rare condition will tend to look weakly connected to a common one even when the link is real.

Where to draw the line

A correlation computed from a couple of hundred people will rarely be exactly zero, even for two conditions with nothing to do with each other. So the study needed a rule for when $\varphi$ is large enough to believe. The standard test for a correlation coefficient converts it into a $t$ statistic,

\[t = \frac{|\varphi|\sqrt{N-2}}{\sqrt{1-\varphi^2}},\]

where $N$ is the number of people behind that pair, and compares it with Student’s $t$ distribution with $N-2$ degrees of freedom. If the conditions were truly unrelated, a $t$ above about 2.35 would happen less than 1% of the time, and that was the rule in the BMC paper: an edge whenever the one-sided p-value was below 0.01 . For a pair answered by around 200 people, that works out to $\varphi$ of roughly 0.16 or more. The edge’s weight is then $\varphi$ itself.

Play with the slider and two things become clear. The first is that the network depends on a choice as well as on the data. At 0.05 there are many more edges, including a few negative ones; at 0.001 the network thins to its strongest bonds. The second is the problem of many tests. The study tested 325 pairs. If none of them were truly related, a threshold of 0.01 would still let through about three edges by chance alone, and we have no way of knowing which three. The usual remedy, a Bonferroni correction, divides the threshold by the number of tests, and if you apply it here the network loses a good part of its edges but keeps its psychiatric core and its strongest links. I think the honest reading is that the strong edges are very unlikely to be flukes, and that any single weak edge (a $\varphi$ near 0.16, resting on a handful of shared people) should be held lightly.

The thesis, and then the paper

A word on the thesis network, which was an earlier version of this analysis and is not quite the same as the paper’s. It had 25 conditions (it did not include “other heart conditions”), 69 edges and a diameter of 5 , and used a different threshold for drawing an edge. The paper’s has 26 conditions, of which 25 have at least one edge, and 65 edges . From here on I use the paper’s network, which is the one that went through peer review.

The map

Here, then, is the network for everyone: 25 conditions with at least one edge, joined by 65 edges, and stroke on its own because none of its associations passed the threshold.

Spend a minute with it before reading on. The first thing I notice every time is the dense knot on one side, the psychiatric conditions and substance use, tied to each other by most of the network’s thickest edges. The strongest associations in the whole network are all there: anxiety with panic attacks ($\varphi = 0.56$), attention deficit disorders with alcoholism (0.53), depression with panic attacks (0.49), anxiety with depression (0.48). The next strongest is dementia with movement disorders (0.42), two neurological conditions of later life off on their own. Then there is a looser web of heart, lung and metabolic conditions on the other side, and a few conditions that seem to sit between.

The matrix beside it is the same information without the drawing: all 325 values of $\varphi$, grouped by type of condition. It is worth looking at for what the network hides. Most cells are pale, meaning most pairs of conditions are close to independent, and the edges are a minority (65 of 325, about one in five). The psychiatric block in the corner is dark almost throughout. And there are a few red cells, negative associations, none of them strong enough to become an edge.

Reading the map

The whole network

Part 2 introduced a set of measures for the shape of a network as a whole. The BMC paper did not report them (it went straight to centrality and clusters), so the values below are computed here, from the published network; the thesis reported them for its own, slightly different, network.

A density of 0.22 means about one in five of all possible links is present. The average path between two conditions is 2.31 steps, and no two are more than 4 apart. A random network of the same size would also have short paths (2.05 on average), because 65 edges among 25 nodes is a lot of wiring, so the short paths on their own do not say much. The clustering is the more telling number: 0.36 here against 0.21 for random networks, meaning a condition’s neighbours are much more likely to be linked to each other than chance would arrange. High clustering with short paths is the signature of what Part 2 called a small world , and this network has a mild case of it, as did the thesis network when Part 2 gave it the same comparison.

The assortativity is $+0.41$: conditions with many links tend to be linked to other conditions with many links. That is the psychiatric core again. The most connected conditions are the psychiatric ones, and they are connected mainly to each other, while the rarer, less connected conditions link among themselves at the edges. On a network of 25 nodes this number rests on few edges, so I would not lean on its exact value, but its sign matches what you can see.

The core

Size the nodes by degree or by triangles and the psychiatric knot dominates. Panic attacks has the most links (10), followed by anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress disorder with 9 each, and the same four sit in the most triangles (panic attacks in 25; depression and PTSD in 23 each). A triangle, three conditions all linked to each other, is the smallest unit of a cluster, and these four are tied into dozens of them. My thesis’s main conclusion was about exactly this: “the critical hub formed by the triangular relationship between mental disorders such as depression, anxiety, and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) and with various other disease comorbidities” .

What does a dense psychiatric core mean? It is not a surprising finding in itself. Psychiatric conditions co-occur heavily in the general population, partly because they share risk factors and partly because the categories themselves overlap (panic attacks are, after all, a common feature of anxiety disorders). It is consistent with what the Frontiers paper found about prevalence, that anxiety, depression and PTSD were among the most common conditions to appear at or after a mild TBI , and with the broader literature on mental health after TBI. What the network adds is the shape: these conditions are each common and they also occur together, so that someone with one of them is quite likely to have several. Eigenvector centrality, which scores a node by the scores of its neighbours, says the same thing in another way: its highest values are panic attacks, depression, PTSD and anxiety, the conditions embedded deepest in the core. Across all conditions it tracks degree closely (the paper reports a correlation of 0.93 between the two ).

The bridges

Betweenness tells a different story, and it is the one the paper chose to follow. Before you size the map by it, make a guess.

The answer is bipolar disorder, among the four, and it is not close. Bipolar disorder was reported by about 7% of people, yet it has the second-highest betweenness in the network (0.157), behind only high cholesterol (0.186), with emphysema third (0.133). Depression, reported by almost a third, is near the middle. The paper put the general point this way: across conditions, betweenness was almost uncorrelated with prevalence ($r = 0.028$), and “despite exhibiting a low prevalence rate, a specific comorbidity could play a vital role in controlling disease transitions by being associated either directly or indirectly with other comorbidities in the network” .

The best analogy I know comes from a study of the world’s airline network. Roger Guimerà and colleagues mapped every pair of cities connected by non-stop flights and found that “the most connected cities are not necessarily the most central” . Anchorage and Port Moresby have few routes, but they ranked among the most central cities in the world by betweenness, because they are the gateways between otherwise isolated regions (Alaska, and the interior of Papua New Guinea) and the rest of the network. Bipolar disorder plays something like that role here. Its links run both into the psychiatric core (anxiety, depression, PTSD, panic attacks, alcoholism) and out to the heart (congestive heart failure, myocardial infarction, high cholesterol), so many of the shortest paths between those two neighbourhoods pass through it. Emphysema does the same between substance use and depression on one side and pneumonia and heart failure on the other.

I want to be careful about what “bridge” means. A shortest path in this network is a chain of statistical associations, not a route that a disease travels along. That bipolar disorder sits between psychiatric and cardiovascular conditions says that people with bipolar disorder in this group were more likely than chance to have conditions from both neighbourhoods. It does not say that bipolar disorder leads to heart disease, or the reverse. Then again, it does flag bipolar disorder as a place where two specialities that rarely talk to each other (psychiatry and cardiology) have patients in common, which is the kind of observation a network is good at producing.

Finding the neighbourhoods

Looking at the map, you can see groups. The question is whether there is a principled way to find them, and here the study borrowed a method from a 2020 study of comorbidities among COVID-19 patients in Mexico by Camarillo-Ramirez and colleagues . It is a cousin of the Girvan–Newman method from Part 2 , which finds communities by repeatedly cutting the edge with the highest betweenness. This one removes nodes instead: find the node with the highest betweenness, take it out, recompute, and repeat until no node’s betweenness is above a threshold. What is left falls apart into pieces, and those are the cores of the clusters. Then each removed node is put back into every cluster it had an edge to. Because a removed node can touch several clusters, clusters can overlap, and a bridge can belong to more than one neighbourhood at once, which for diseases seems right to me.

The paper’s supplement illustrates this on a seven-node example, and it is the clearest way to see each step.

The threshold in the BMC paper was the median betweenness of the starting network, a choice the supplement explains after mentioning that minimum, median and user-chosen values were all tried . The rebuild found that a threshold around 0.046 reproduces every published removal sequence, and for the three BMC networks the median falls within the range that works. On the real network, the method removes seven conditions in turn: high cholesterol, emphysema, liver disease, bipolar disorder, rheumatoid arthritis, other heart conditions and attention deficit disorders. Notice how the ranking reshuffles after each removal. Rheumatoid arthritis starts with modest betweenness, but once the conditions around it are gone it becomes the only link between its neighbours, and its score jumps to 0.48 before it is removed in turn.

For everyone, the method finds six clusters, and they are the paper’s six . The first is the psychiatric core (alcoholism, anxiety, depression, drug addiction, PTSD, panic attacks) with chronic pain and sleep disorder, plus five bridges put back in: attention deficit disorders, bipolar disorder, emphysema, liver disease and rheumatoid arthritis. The paper read it as reinforcing that psychiatric conditions are highly comorbid, and noted that emphysema’s links were to depression, alcoholism and drug addiction. The second pairs diabetes and cataracts, with high cholesterol, liver disease and other heart conditions as bridges. The third is obsessive-compulsive disorder with attention deficit disorders and rheumatoid arthritis, notable because OCD is otherwise unconnected to the psychiatric core. The fourth is a heart and lung cluster around congestive heart failure, myocardial infarction and pneumonia, which is where bipolar disorder’s cardiovascular links live. The fifth joins dementia, hypertension and movement disorders, and the sixth is osteoarthritis with high cholesterol.

Younger and older

The thesis stopped at one network. The question that drove the BMC paper was whether the network looks different depending on age, which matters for a condition like TBI because the people it happens to differ so much: a fall at 75 and a road accident at 25 happen to different bodies, with different conditions already waiting in the wings. The Frontiers paper had already found that, at five years, younger people reported depression more often and older people reported hypertension, high cholesterol, cataracts and osteoarthritis more often , a pattern close to what an earlier TBIMS study found ten years after moderate and severe injuries . So the paper split the 225 at age 50 and built a network for each group.

The two networks are clearly different. The younger network (91 people, 48 edges among 21 conditions) is held together by panic attacks, which has 12 links, more than any condition anywhere else in the study, and its assortativity is negative ($-0.20$), meaning its well-connected conditions tend to link to poorly connected ones, hub and spokes. The older network (134 people, 37 edges among 22 conditions) is sparser and splits into two pieces, with dementia and movement disorders on their own, and its assortativity is $+0.44$. In the older group, anxiety and depression become the bridges the clustering method removes first; in the younger, it is panic attacks, stroke and depression.

The paper’s abstract leads with one difference: “bipolar disorder was seen as related to cardiovascular comorbidities, a pattern that was observed only in the young subjects” . In the younger network, bipolar disorder is linked to myocardial infarction, congestive heart failure and high cholesterol; in the older network it has no cardiovascular links at all. This is not without precedent. The paper points to an American Heart Association scientific statement that bipolar disorder and major depression predispose young people to early cardiovascular disease, and to a nationwide Korean cohort in which young adults with bipolar disorder had a raised risk of heart attack . The second difference is obsessive-compulsive disorder linked with rheumatoid arthritis (and with attention deficit disorders) in the younger group only, which the paper connects to evidence that OCD may involve inflammation and is associated with autoimmune conditions in a Swedish nationwide study. Third, which non-psychiatric conditions the psychiatric ones connect to depends on age: liver disease is linked to anxiety and PTSD only in the younger group, and chronic pain to drug addiction, panic attacks and PTSD only in the older.

I want to be honest about how much weight these can bear. The younger network rests on 91 people, and some of its conditions were reported by fewer than 11 of them. Stroke is a good example: in the younger network it has seven links and the second-highest betweenness, but fewer than 11 younger people reported it, so a few individuals with several conditions each can produce all of those edges. The bipolar–cardiovascular links in the young may be real, and they fit the literature, but they rest on small numbers, and I would treat them as a hypothesis worth testing in a larger cohort rather than as a finding to act on. The paper itself says the sample “could be even lower when considering patient subgroups” .

What it means, and what it does not

The argument for using networks

Why go to all this trouble? The perspective paper Dr Sudhakar and I wrote makes the case. TBI is followed by a multitude of psychiatric and medical conditions over the long term, and there are no medicines that prevent the secondary injuries that follow the first impact, so a good deal of what can be done for people is managing what comes after. In its own words: “we propose applying graph theory via the construction of disease comorbidity networks to identify high-risk patient groups, offer preventive care to affected populations, and reduce the disease burden” . The BMC paper adds the practical problem behind it: continued surveillance of TBI survivors “for all possible sets of comorbidities is impractical due to the associated costs and the wide range of comorbidities”, so “a more practical and economical way to monitor comorbidities in TBI subjects is required” .

A network suggests where to look. If you know that, in young people after a mild TBI, bipolar disorder tends to come with heart problems, then a young patient with bipolar disorder is someone whose heart might be worth checking earlier than usual, and that is the paper’s main suggestion for practice. Larger studies point in the same direction: a cohort study of people with mild TBI followed for up to ten years found raised risks of hypertension, diabetes and stroke compared with uninjured people , and its authors called for screening for these conditions after TBI. And the general idea has deep roots in network medicine: in the Hidalgo study, patients tended to develop diseases close in the network to those they already had . If that holds after TBI, a comorbidity network is a rough map of where a patient might be heading.

That is what I hope these networks could become. What they show at the moment is much narrower.

What the study cannot tell us

It cannot say which came first. An edge says two conditions occur together more than chance; it says nothing about direction. The BMC paper was explicit: “if there is an association between comorbidities A and B in the study, one won’t be able to establish if A preceded B or B preceded A” . The network is undirected because the data cannot support arrows. Hidalgo’s study could infer direction because it had records of successive hospital visits ; one set of yes-or-no answers at five years cannot.

It cannot say the injury caused any of this. There is no comparison group of similar people without a brain injury, so we cannot tell which associations are peculiar to TBI and which would appear in any group of people of the same age. Anxiety and depression go together in almost every population. The paper’s answer is that the aim was to document the patterns in people with mild TBI regardless of their cause, since they matter for those people either way, and it also argues that choosing controls is complicated by evidence that brains age faster after TBI . I think both points are fair, and I also think a control group is the single thing that would most change what this network could claim.

The conditions are self-reported, as diagnoses a doctor gave, as the person recalls them. People who see doctors more get diagnosed with more things, and people may misremember what they were told or when.

The people are a particular slice of TBI. They were hospitalised and then had inpatient rehabilitation in the United States, they survived five years, they were interviewed, and their interview fell between 2017 and 2019. The Frontiers paper warned that “sufficient caution should be exercised while generalizing the results of the study to the mild TBI population as a whole” . And survivorship cuts both ways: people who died or dropped out are invisible, and if they were the sickest, the network shows a healthier picture than the reality.

The network depends on choices: the 1% threshold, with 325 pairs tested and so some edges likely to be false positives, $\varphi$ rather than relative risk, the median threshold in the clustering. Each is defensible, and each could reasonably have been made differently, as the slider above shows.

The numbers are small, especially in the age groups, and conditions reported by fewer than 11 people (several of them, in each group) can gain or lose edges from one or two individuals.

Beyond the paper

The thesis ended with a line I would still stand by: the choice of mild TBI at five years was arbitrary, and “future research will focus on integrating data across TBI severities and longitudinal scales” . The original code had in fact already computed networks for other severities and other years, though they were never analysed. The rebuild recomputed them, and I show them here as an exploratory figure, clearly outside anything the papers claim.

It is tempting to read the rows as a story told over fifteen years, and that is precisely the reading the data does not support. Each cell is a cross-section of different people, of different sizes (from 53 to 384), so differences between cells mix the passage of time with who happened to be asked. What the grid does show is that the psychiatric core is not peculiar to mild injuries at five years: something like it appears in most cells, which makes me more inclined to believe it is a stable feature of life after TBI rather than an accident of one sample. The rest I would treat as a set of hypotheses.

Open questions

What I would do next, given the time and the data, is the work the thesis promised and did not do. The first is to follow the same people across years, so that an edge could carry a direction: if depression tends to be reported at two years and heart problems at ten, in the same people, that is a much stronger statement than both being present at five. The second is to build the same networks for people without a brain injury, matched on age and sex, and look at the difference, which is where anything specific to TBI would have to show up. The third is to compare severities properly, with enough people in each group to say whether the network’s shape changes with the force of the injury. Each of these needs more data than an undergraduate project had access to, and the BMC paper’s own stated aim, to build a large database of TBI patients and their follow-up across trauma centres in India , is the version of this I would most like to see.

And some questions I do not know how to answer. Is the psychiatric core a feature of brain injury, or a feature of people, which any network of conditions would show? Is bipolar disorder a bridge to the heart in young people because of something shared in their biology (inflammation, metabolism, the medicines used to treat it) or because of how and when young people with bipolar disorder see doctors? If betweenness picks out conditions that sit between specialities, could it be used to decide which specialists a patient should see, and would that help anyone? How much would the map change if the questions had been asked every year, to everyone, rather than to the 225 whose interview fell in the right three years? I suspect the answers matter more than any single edge in the network, and I hope someone finds them curious enough to take up.

This work began as my undergraduate capstone at Krea University, and I am properly thankful to Dr Shyam Kumar Sudhakar, who supervised it, conceived the papers that grew from it and did much of the writing; and to Shreya Sridhar, Satvika Char and Kathan Pandya, co-authors of the prevalence paper. The data come from the TBIMS National Database, funded by the National Institute on Disability, Independent Living, and Rehabilitation Research, and from the people with brain injuries who answered its questions for years. The papers are open access: the networks in BMC Neurology , the prevalences in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience , and the perspective in the Brain Organoid and Systems Neuroscience Journal . The aggregated data behind every figure here, with notes on how each file was made, are in the site’s repository.

entry.title: Bread, butter and a WhatsApp prescription

entry.content:
“Of course, we cannot give bread and butter for all 6000 patients. But we gave provisions for about 300 of them through various sources.” A manager heading outreach at the Schizophrenia Research Foundation, Chennai, on the months after India’s 2020 lockdown

That sentence is from an interview with a service provider at the Schizophrenia Research Foundation (SCARF), a non-government organisation in Chennai that provides care for a range of mental disorders and runs outreach services for rural communities. It is an odd thing to hear from a mental health organisation, because food is not usually counted as part of mental health care. The paper places it in a section on the burden of care at home, where the closure of the vocational centre and day-care came on top of job loss, pay cuts and rising debt for caregivers, and read in that context I find it hard to see where mental health care was supposed to stop and the rest of a family’s troubles begin.

This post is about my first research paper, The COVID-19 pandemic and its impact on mental health services: the provider perspective, published in the Journal of Public Health in October 2021 . It came out of a partnership between LEAD at Krea University and the University of Oxford, funded through the Global Challenges Research Fund’s India–Oxford Initiative, and it asked a fairly simple question: when the country shut down, what happened to community mental health services, and how did the people providing them keep them running?

I should say up front what my part in it was. The interviews, the focus group and the thematic analysis were done by my co-authors. My part was the literature review, which meant reading what had been reported from a geographically and socio-economically spread set of countries and using it to place the Chennai data in a wider context. The journal format is tight, about six pages, and most of the participants’ words had to be cut down to fragments. So, five years on, I wanted to write about it in a form where the quotes get more room and some of the numbers can be drawn out. How the study was done, and what was happening elsewhere at the time, come later in the post; Chennai comes first.

What broke

The first thing to go was access. In the two weeks of complete lockdown, in the paper’s words, “all services were affected”, and even once essential services resumed, patients could not easily reach the centre. Not every neighbourhood pharmacy stocked psychiatric medication, and some pharmacists that did were reluctant to dispense it. In smaller towns, psychiatric care was taken over for COVID-19 treatment. Rural patients were stopped by the police and fined on their way to refill prescriptions at SCARF, even when they showed the prescription.

“These are people who can’t even afford medicines… it felt painful that we were helpless.” A manager heading outreach efforts (P6)

Missed medication meant relapses of conditions like schizophrenia and mood disorders, often needing in-patient care, at exactly the time the centre had stopped admissions for fear of spreading COVID-19 inside the facility. One of the psychiatrists recalled handling “at least ten DESPERATE requests for admissions” (the capitals are in the paper). For patients who had been discharged and rehabilitated, the closure of the vocational centre took away a daily routine as well. The same psychiatrist described the “11 o clock tea” and the people they talked to, and added that most of them keep in touch with the staff regularly: “It was sad for them because this was their social life…” For people living with a chronic mental illness, I suspect that routine and that company were doing some of the work of treatment, even if nobody would have written them into a care plan.

What they built instead

What I find most interesting, reading the paper again, is how ordinary the adaptations were. Prescriptions were written on the official pad, signed, photographed and sent over WhatsApp, in line with the teleconsultation guidelines, and the consultants then spent time on the phone with pharmacists sorting out legibility, brand names, durations and substitutes. A health worker contacted the doctors of clients who were stuck in other districts and passed their prescriptions on. One psychiatrist described calling a pharmacist herself to get an overdue prescription honoured, asking them to dispense “for 1 week or 10 days” until she could see the patient.

That last detail is where my part of the paper meets the data. In the literature I was reviewing, one of the adaptations other health systems had made was to let patients keep using expired prescriptions . The same idea turns up in Chennai, except that here it was not a policy. It was one psychiatrist’s phone call, and it worked as long as she had the time and the pharmacist was willing.

The centre also ran a 24-hour helpline that linked new and existing patients to consultants and therapists. It was open to the public for distress calls, and the government displayed it in its media advertisements, so an NGO’s line became, in effect, part of the public response. The paper notes the cost plainly: existing staff and doctors had their working hours extended to handle the calls. It does not say whether that work was funded, so I will not guess, but it does make me wonder who carries the cost when a public service runs on an organisation’s goodwill.

Some of the infrastructure was even more personal. In the in-patient centres, staff used their own phones to set up video calls with families, partly to settle patients made anxious by the news coverage of COVID-19, and because many patients did not have smartphones. When staff or patients with cards and e-passes were stopped by the police, an administrator would be handed the phone to vouch for them. Decisions, emotional support and the sharing of load all happened in WhatsApp groups. Putting these together (and this is my synthesis, not the paper’s), a good part of the organisation’s continuity ran through its employees’ personal phones.

One of the most concrete changes in clinical practice was time. One psychiatrist described how a first consultation for a new patient, which used to take an hour, was now done in fifteen to twenty minutes.

A natural reading of that number is that care got worse, and I do not think the paper lets us say that. The time with the psychiatrist shrank, but the work was redistributed. A case manager took basic case details on a first phone call, and after the shorter consultation a case worker called the patient back to take the detailed history, which the psychiatrist then read at the next visit. The patient’s story was now held together by a case manager, a psychiatrist, a case worker and the electronic record, rather than by one person in one room. Whether that amounted to a loss, a different kind of care, or in some cases a better use of a psychiatrist’s hour is something interviews with providers alone cannot settle.

What it cost the people carrying it

The paper has a section on the providers’ personal costs, which I think is easy to skim past and should not be, partly because most of those costs follow directly from the adaptations above. The helpline extended working hours. The personal phones never went quiet. An administrative co-ordinator said that the hours after half past four used to be her own, and that she now checked her phone every three to five minutes “because I don’t want to miss anything”. Providers described feeling torn between giving good care and carrying out the new procedures, worried about bringing the virus home to their families, and saw less of their colleagues.

Some of it also cut across the usual hierarchy. The paper notes that responding meant “working across hierarchies”, and that two or three of the respondents held senior management positions on top of their other roles, which goes some way to explaining why a psychiatrist was negotiating with a pharmacist and an administrator was talking to the police.

The paper is also clear about why they kept going: commitment to care “was based on their personal motivation, a perceived sense of fulfilment”, despite the long hours and what it did to their work-life balance. I find that reassuring and a little worrying at once. If an organisation’s resilience rests on the motivation and overtime of its staff, how long can it last when the crisis does not end after two weeks? The study did not measure burnout, so I can only leave that as a question.

Telemedicine, and the room it took away

Telemedicine was the largest single change. The paper’s abstract says it enabled an expansion of both the service and its clientele, as well as efficiency, and the gains were real. It also changed what a therapy session was like, for both sides.

The phrase “casualization” is the one I keep coming back to.The abstract uses “casualization of therapy”; the discussion uses “casualization of the exchange between service provider and patient”. Some clients, as the paper puts it, took phone sessions as “a friendly catch-up call rather than a teletherapy session”. A case worker said that when she asked clients why they had not called, they told her they thought the centre had called “just to ask ‘How are you doing? Are you taking medicine’”. I wonder whether that is partly a side effect of the relationship itself. Years of check-in calls teach people that a call from SCARF is a kind voice asking how they are, and when therapy arrived through the same phone, it is not surprising that some heard it the same way. The work of keeping to a schedule also moved from the client to the counsellor, which the paper counts as an additional burden.

The cost I did not appreciate until I sat with these quotes is privacy. A consulting room is, among other things, a private space, and it is easy not to notice that until it is gone. One outreach manager described families where “women and children have faced a lot of issues”, and asked how a woman could talk about her husband to someone over the phone when the husband was in the room. Moving care into the home moved it, for some women, into the very place where the problem was. The paper makes the general point in its discussion, that privacy issues may matter most “in planning for communities with space constraints”, and I think that one line deserves more weight than its place in the discussion suggests. I should be careful about how far it goes, though: this is one provider’s account of what women could not say, not the women’s own words, and the study cannot tell us how common it was.

Privacy failed at the other end of the line too. The counsellor whose children “would wonder why the person on the other end was crying so much” was describing a cost to herself, and the paper files it that way, under her loss of privacy and family time. I think it was also a cost to the person crying, whose distress was audible to a stranger’s parents and children without anyone having chosen that. The same outreach manager noticed his own position: “I am sitting and talking to you in a sound proof room, but that is not possible for everyone.”In the paper, that remark sits in a passage about public outreach and training moving online, where it was harder to keep up two-way communication with community health workers in rural districts. He goes on: “Women in rural areas were not comfortable with gadgets.” I have used only the first sentence here, as an observation about privacy.

The crowded home that took privacy away also turned family into a resource. Compliance was better where family members became co-therapists, and one patient was rehabilitated with the help of her 10-year-old child. The paper presents that as a success, and it may well have been one. I would only ask, as a question rather than a criticism, what we are asking of a ten-year-old when we make them part of their parent’s treatment.

Relationships, responsiveness, resilience

When the paper pulls these threads together, it names “three crucial elements in continuity and quality service delivery: relationships, responsiveness and resilience” .

Two of the three were in place before the pandemic. The relationships had been built over many years, partly through educating patients and families, and the providers felt that this psycho-education showed its value in how well patients kept to treatment. The resilience drew on lessons from earlier floods, the tsunami and cyclones, and on prior experience with tele-psychiatry, which the paper says made the move online easier. Responsiveness is the one that happened during the crisis, in the continual adaptations described above. I suspect the first two are what made the third possible: provisions can only reach 300 patients if someone already knows who those patients are. The paper does not say which lessons from the earlier disasters carried over, and I would genuinely like to know, because a pandemic is a different kind of disaster, long and everywhere at once, with no unaffected place from which help can arrive.

The view from outside

None of this was unique to Chennai in kind. In October 2020 the World Health Organization published a survey of 130 countries , and the headline figure was blunt.

The literature I was reading at the time was largely about hospitals and health systems. From China there were accounts of psychiatric hospitals reorganising around infection control , and elsewhere descriptions of how inpatient psychiatry and psychiatric care more broadly had been reshaped in the first months . A piece in The Lancet Psychiatry set out how mental health care should change as a consequence . Adaptation was not absent from this work: telecommunication platforms, electronic prescriptions, the continued use of expired prescriptions, isolation and liaison psychiatry were all being reported . What was missing was adaptation in community care run by NGOs, which matters in India because mental health outreach to communities and vulnerable groups here was pioneered by NGOs, and their lessons have proved useful to the public system .

Reading that literature against the Chennai interviews, a few comparisons stand out to me. The expired-prescription policy elsewhere and the psychiatrist’s phone call to a pharmacist are one. Another is the observation that services for rural and older populations, which were always harder to reach, got worse during the pandemic , set against rural patients being fined on their way to collect medicine. A third is the WHO’s split in telemedicine adoption between high- and low-income countries, set against the women in shared homes who could not speak freely on a call. In each case the broad pattern in the literature shows up in Chennai, but at the scale of a single person and a single phone call.

In India specifically, services were disrupted by the nationwide lockdown in March 2020, and the government released guidelines to move to telemedicine . Tele-psychiatry had raised concerns about patient dynamics, proper diagnosis and legal issues , though it had worked in some contexts .

How the study was done

SCARF is, in the paper’s words, a training centre for psychiatry, psychology and psychiatric social work, and a training partner for public mental health services, as well as a provider . That breadth meant one organisation’s staff could speak about many kinds of service, from inpatient wards to rural outreach. The paper also notes the organisation’s prior experience with tele-psychiatry, which probably left it better placed than many.

The people interviewed included managers of clinical services, administrative staff, psychiatrists, social workers, a psychologist and research staff, with between three and more than twenty years at the organisation. Their accounts covered February to December 2020, and the fieldwork itself ran over December 2020 and January 2021. One small thing I should flag: the paper says ten providers were selected and that one interview could not be scheduled, yet quotes are labelled up to P10, so the numbering may not map neatly onto the interviews that took place.

What this study cannot tell us

The paper is direct about its main limitation: “Though limited to a single NGO and to providers, insights from a variety of services within mental healthcare was gleaned” . Both halves of that sentence matter. One organisation based in one city, however broad its services and however far its outreach reaches, is not Indian community mental health care as a whole. And the people interviewed were the people delivering care, not receiving it. We do not know how the shortened consultation felt from the patient’s side, or whether the phone sessions that providers worried were too casual felt that way to the people on the other end.

It is also a retrospective account. The interviews were conducted at the end of 2020 about the months that came before, and what people remember of a crisis, and how they make sense of it afterwards, is not quite the same as what happened at the time. I would rather say that plainly than have the post read as a claim about more than the study can support.

Coming back to it

The paper ends by arguing that these insights are crucial for planning resilient community-based mental health care, and the wider literature at the time was saying something similar: that the pandemic was an opportunity to reform mental health care in India , and that health systems needed to be built with preparedness in mind . The paper is specific about what that would mean: bringing care for people with mental illness into government and city disaster planning, including housing, transport and medication; sensitising the police and other enforcing authorities to their needs, which I read as coming out of the patients fined at checkpoints; training health workers for isolation, infection and relocation; and preparing patients and caregivers for how to manage care during a disaster.

Reading it again now, the question I keep returning to is which of these adaptations outlasted the pandemic, and whether anyone asked patients what the phone intake, the shorter consultation and the WhatsApp prescription changed for them. I do not have an answer, and I suspect it needs the patient and family perspective this study did not have. That includes the families who were not among the 300, and I would like to know what they made of the year.

It was my first time seeing my name on a paper, and I am properly thankful to my co-authors, Sapna Nair, Preethi Kannan, Ananya Raju, John Mathew and Padmavati Ramachandran, for bringing me in, and to the providers at SCARF who gave their time to be interviewed at the end of a very hard year. The full paper is available from the Journal of Public Health.
